title: A Non-Commutative Voronovskaya Theorem for Quantum Neural Network Operators
summary:
We prove a complete asymptotic expansion for quantum neural network operators when they approximate arbitrary quantum channels. This is the non-commutative analogue of the classical Voronovskaya theorem. The expansion reveals that the approximation error splits into three fundamentally different parts: integer powers of \(1/n\) involving ordinary Fréchet derivatives; fractional powers governed by Marchaud fractional derivatives, which capture the Hölder smoothness of the channel; and purely quantum commutator terms that have no classical counterpart. The remainder is bounded sharply by an explicit constant:
  \[
  \norm{R_{m,n}(Φ,\bullet)}_\diamond \le C_{m,γ,d} \|Φ\|_{\cC^{m,γ}} \, n^{-(m+γ)} (\log n)^{3m/2}.
  \]
  We present a numerical test for a classical analogue that confirms the predicted convergence rate and the logarithmic correction, directly validating the asymptotic theory. Based on this expansion, we obtain three major advances: a quantum central limit theorem for the fluctuations of quantum neural network operators, a method to construct optimal interpolation geodesics between quantum channels via Kubo-Ando means, and a systematic understanding of how fractional smoothness limits the acceleration of quantum neural network approximations. The numerical test further demonstrates that the theoretical rates are sharp and that logarithmic enhancements are unavoidable. Altogether, our work builds a rigorous bridge between classical approximation theory, fractional calculus, and quantum machine learning, offering both theoretical insight and practical tools for designing and analyzing quantum neural networks in finite dimensions.

AI.tldr: This paper proves a complete asymptotic expansion for quantum neural network operators approximating arbitrary quantum channels, establishing the non-commutative analogue of the classical Voronovskaya theorem, with error terms split into integer-order Fréchet derivatives, fractional Marchaud derivatives capturing Hölder smoothness, and purely quantum commutator terms. The expansion yields a quantum central limit theorem, optimal interpolation geodesics via Kubo-Ando means, and insights into fractional smoothness limitations for acceleration, with numerical validation of sharp rates and unavoidable logarithmic corrections.
AI.motivation: To develop a rigorous asymptotic theory for quantum neural network operators analogous to classical approximation theory, bridging the gap between classical approximation theory, fractional calculus, and quantum machine learning, while providing both theoretical foundations and practical tools for designing and analyzing quantum neural networks.
AI.method: The authors prove a complete asymptotic expansion for quantum neural network operators approximating arbitrary quantum channels, analyzing the error decomposition into three components: integer powers of 1/n with Fréchet derivatives, fractional powers with Marchaud fractional derivatives (capturing Hölder smoothness), and quantum commutator terms. They derive a sharp remainder bound with explicit constant, validate the theory with numerical tests on a classical analogue, and apply the expansion to obtain three major theoretical advances.
AI.result: The expansion shows approximation error splits into three parts: integer-power terms from Fréchet derivatives, fractional-power terms from Marchaud derivatives reflecting Hölder smoothness, and purely quantum commutator terms. The remainder is bounded by \(\|R_{m,n}(\Phi,\cdot)\|_\diamond \le C_{m,\gamma,d} \|\Phi\|_{\mathcal{C}^{m,\gamma}} n^{-(m+\gamma)} (\log n)^{3m/2}\). Numerical tests confirm predicted convergence rates and logarithmic corrections. The work yields a quantum central limit theorem, optimal interpolation geodesics via Kubo-Ando means, and understanding of how fractional smoothness limits acceleration.
AI.conclusion: The work builds a rigorous bridge between classical approximation theory, fractional calculus, and quantum machine learning, offering both theoretical insight and practical tools for designing and analyzing quantum neural networks in finite dimensions. The asymptotic theory is sharp with unavoidable logarithmic enhancements.

title: What It Is Like To Be A Quantum Computer: A Closed Quantum Global Workspace -- Conscious Access and Integration as Correlation Dynamics in Hilbert Space
summary:
Motivated by speculative artistic inquiry into quantum-only forms of experience in relation to representation and embodiment, this paper develops a translation of the Global Neuronal Workspace (GNW) theory for closed quantum systems. The work treats classical GNW as an architectural reference and asks how conscious access and memory change under unitary dynamics.
  We reference a quantum Hopfield-style Hamiltonian that mirrors key organisational features of GNW, such as a distributed workspace and tunable large-scale integration. Within this framework, global availability of information is realised through coherence-preserving correlation distributions and memory is a persistent internal correlation structure. Likewise, ignition becomes a transition in global entanglement as opposed to convergence towards a stable attractor. Reductions of the Hopfield-style Hamiltonian lead to a tractable toy model and GHZ-type entanglement, explicitly showing how relative phase is globally accessible through joint internal operations yet absent from all local subsystems.
  This closed quantum system approach clarifies which aspects of workspace theories are contingent on classical assumptions. Our model highlights a non-representational regime in which access and memory are entirely relational rather than copies or records.
  Beyond its scientific contribution, the paper proposes a mode of art-science collaboration where speculative artistic inquiry is pursued through theoretical models rather than illustration or data.

AI.tldr: This paper translates Global Neuronal Workspace (GNW) theory into a closed quantum system framework using a quantum Hopfield-style Hamiltonian, showing how conscious access and memory become coherence-preserving correlation structures and entanglement transitions rather than classical attractor dynamics, revealing a non-representational regime where access and memory are entirely relational.
AI.motivation: Motivated by speculative artistic inquiry into quantum-only forms of experience in relation to representation and embodiment, the paper aims to translate GNW theory into a closed quantum system to clarify which aspects of workspace theories are contingent on classical assumptions.
AI.method: The paper uses a quantum Hopfield-style Hamiltonian that mirrors GNW's organizational features (distributed workspace, tunable large-scale integration). Reductions of this Hamiltonian lead to a tractable toy model with GHZ-type entanglement.
AI.result: Global availability is realized through coherence-preserving correlation distributions; memory is a persistent internal correlation structure; ignition becomes a transition in global entanglement rather than convergence to a stable attractor. Relative phase is globally accessible through joint internal operations yet absent from all local subsystems.
AI.conclusion: The model highlights a non-representational regime where access and memory are entirely relational rather than copies or records. Beyond science, the paper proposes art-science collaboration where speculative artistic inquiry is pursued through theoretical models rather than illustration or data.

title: Comment on Temperature change can solve the Deutsch-Jozsa problem: An exploration of thermodynamic query complexity
summary: We show that the readout analysis in Phys. Rev. A 113, 012420 (2026) does not establish the claimed resource accounting of one thermal query followed by many statistically useful probe samples. A CNOT fanout of a diagonal post-query probe broadcasts its one-qubit marginal but produces perfectly correlated registers rather than independent copies. Consequently, neither the trace distance nor the relative entropy between the balanced and constant hypotheses increases, and repeated measurements of the ancillas provide only one Bernoulli observation. Independent samples instead require repeated preparation and heat exchange, which are repeated queries under the definition adopted in the original paper. We also show that the sample lower bound stated there does not follow from Pinsker's inequality: the inequality gives the opposite ordering for the reciprocal relative entropy. The thermal-kickback mechanism may still encode the decision in the probe temperature, but the one-query readout claim and the quoted necessity of approximately 116 samples require correction.

AI.tldr: This paper critiques a previous work (Phys. Rev. A 113, 012420, 2026), arguing that its claimed resource accounting—specifically that one thermal query can yield many statistically useful probe samples—is flawed. The CNOT fanout produces correlated registers, not independent copies; thus trace distance and relative entropy do not improve. Repeated measurements yield only one Bernoulli observation, and independent samples require repeated queries. The sample lower bound derived from Pinsker's inequality is also incorrect due to reversed ordering. The original claims about one-query readout and ~116 samples need correction.
AI.motivation: To correct erroneous claims in a previously published paper regarding the number of queries needed for thermal readout in quantum information processing, specifically that one thermal query followed by many probe samples is insufficient due to correlation and statistical limitations.
AI.method: The authors analyze the readout protocol from the target paper, demonstrating that a CNOT fanout produces perfectly correlated registers (not independent copies), that trace distance and relative entropy do not increase with multiple measurements, and that Pinsker's inequality is misapplied (it gives the opposite ordering for reciprocal relative entropy).
AI.result: The one-query readout claim is invalid because: (1) the CNOT fanout creates correlated rather than independent copies; (2) repeated measurements yield only a single Bernoulli observation; (3) independent samples require repeated queries; (4) the sample lower bound from Pinsker's inequality is incorrectly derived (the inequality yields opposite ordering).
AI.conclusion: The thermal-kickback mechanism may still encode a decision in probe temperature, but the specific one-query readout claim and the stated necessity of ~116 samples are incorrect and require correction.

title: Comment on Statistical mechanics from quantum envariance and exchange symmetry
summary: Ojha, Sardana, and Ghosh [Phys. Rev. A 113, 042221 (2026)] propose that tracing environmental records of particle permutations produces an entropy kB ln N!, thereby explaining the Gibbs factor, and use the same construction to multiply the Saha equilibrium relation by 1/(Ne!Np!). We show that these conclusions do not follow. The reduced density matrix printed in their Eq. (32) is not a partial trace, and even under the natural corrected interpretation the entropy equals kB ln N! only when the system branch states are mutually orthogonal. That condition is not generally satisfied and, when imposed on labeled permutation branches, does not by itself restrict the particle state to one bosonic or fermionic symmetry sector. A two-particle calculation makes the contradiction explicit. Their Gibbs-paradox calculation also starts from a distinguishable-particle entropy while calling it the Sackur-Tetrode entropy. In the Saha section, the state in Eq. (52), as written, factorizes and has zero system-environment entanglement. The proposed factorial does not approach unity in the claimed dilute-gas limit, does not yield a finite nonzero intensive thermodynamic limit, and counts indistinguishability twice. We give the corrected canonical and fugacity-based formulations and identify which standard results of the paper remain unaffected.

AI.tldr: This paper refutes a recent proposal by Ojha, Sardana, and Ghosh that tracing over permutation records yields entropy kB ln N! and explains the Gibbs factor. The authors show the proposed reduced density matrix is not a proper partial trace, the entropy result holds only under unrealistic orthogonality conditions, the Gibbs paradox and Saha equilibrium calculations contain fundamental errors, and the claimed factorial does not yield correct thermodynamic limits.
AI.motivation: To critically examine and correct erroneous claims by Ojha et al. regarding the origin of the Gibbs factor (1/N!) from environmental entanglement entropy, and to identify which standard results of their paper remain valid.
AI.method: The authors analyze the mathematical structure of the proposed reduced density matrix (Eq. 32), test the entropy claim against the condition of mutual orthogonality of branch states, perform a two-particle explicit calculation to expose contradictions, examine the Gibbs paradox and Saha equilibrium derivations for logical and mathematical consistency, and provide corrected canonical and fugacity-based formulations.
AI.result: The reduced density matrix in Eq. (32) is not a valid partial trace; the entropy equals kB ln N! only when system branch states are mutually orthogonal, which is not generally satisfied and does not restrict to bosonic/fermionic symmetry sectors; the two-particle calculation shows explicit contradiction; the Gibbs paradox derivation uses distinguishable-particle entropy while calling it Sackur-Tetrode; the Saha state in Eq. (52) factorizes with zero entanglement; the proposed factorial does not approach unity in the dilute-gas limit, does not yield a finite intensive thermodynamic limit, and double-counts indistinguishability.
AI.conclusion: The claims of Ojha et al. are fundamentally flawed and do not provide a valid explanation for the Gibbs factor via environmental entanglement entropy. The authors provide corrected formulations while noting that certain standard results in the original paper remain unaffected.

title: Double Covariance Model for Entangled Quantum States: Gaussian Reduction to Second Order Covariances
comment: Invited talk at QIP26 conference, Vaxjoe, June 2026
summary: We propose a novel approach to the problem of interconnecting the probabilistic formalisms of classical and quantum physics, focusing on its most challenging aspect: the classical probabilistic generation of entangled states. We show that the statistics encoded in the density operators of composite quantum systems correspond to fourth-order classical statistics. Specifically, to generate a density operator, one must consider the covariance of a random covariance operator. We term this framework the Double Covariance Model (DCM). This double covariance possesses a non-trivial internal structure that arises from the interplay between two distinct time scales, combining temporal and statistical covariances. In this article, we exploit a well-known property of Gaussian processes: the second-order moment determines the moments of higher orders, specifically the fourth-order moment. This Gaussian reduction simplifies the DCM by reducing it to second-order statistics. Utilizing (circular) Gaussian processes simplifies and generalizes the DCM construction for entangled states, rendering it mathematically rigorous. Furthermore, it clarifies the classical probabilistic meaning of concurrence, a foundational quantitative measure of entanglement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Double Covariance Model (DCM), a classical probabilistic framework that links classical and quantum physics by showing that quantum density operators correspond to fourth-order classical statistics, specifically the covariance of a random covariance operator. Using Gaussian processes, the model reduces to second-order statistics, enabling rigorous generation of entangled states and clarifying the probabilistic meaning of concurrence.
AI.motivation: To bridge classical and quantum probabilistic formalisms by addressing the challenge of generating entangled states from a classical probabilistic perspective.
AI.method: The Double Covariance Model (DCM) treats quantum density operators as fourth-order classical statistics (covariance of a random covariance operator), and exploits Gaussian process properties to reduce fourth-order moments to second-order statistics, simplifying the construction.
AI.result: The DCM framework, when reduced via circular Gaussian processes, provides a mathematically rigorous classical probabilistic construction for entangled states and clarifies the classical meaning of concurrence.
AI.conclusion: The double covariance structure, combining temporal and statistical covariances, offers a classical probabilistic foundation for quantum entanglement, with Gaussian reduction enabling tractable analysis.

title: On the Experimental Determination of Nonlocal Characteristics of Two-Qubit Gates
comment: 7 pages. Research in progress. Comments are welcome
summary: In this paper, we discuss the experimental determination of the nonlocal characteristics of two-qubit gates. Based on the recently derived expressions for the entangling power and gate typicality of two-qubit gates, we construct two-qubit quantum circuits to measure the entangling power and gate typicality of the two-qubit gates, which are generated by the elements of the su(4) Cartan subalgebra. These elements describe the native interactions in many quantum processors. Hence, these circuits can be used to determine the nonlocal characteristics of native gates of many quantum processors. In each circuit, the native gate is applied twice. In addition, each circuit consists of at least one CNOT gate. A set of six two-qubit circuits is constructed to measure the entangling power. The number of circuits is further reduced to three by increasing the nonlocal resources (the number of CNOT gates). To measure the gate typicality, a set of three two-qubit circuits is constructed. Measurement of gate typicality requires more nonlocal resources than the measurement of entangling power.

AI.tldr: The paper presents experimental methods to determine nonlocal characteristics (entangling power and gate typicality) of two-qubit gates using specifically designed quantum circuits. These circuits apply native gates twice and include CNOT gates, with sets of 6 (or 3 with more CNOTs) circuits for entangling power and 3 circuits for gate typicality.
AI.motivation: To experimentally determine the nonlocal characteristics (entangling power and gate typicality) of two-qubit gates based on recently derived theoretical expressions, enabling characterization of native interactions in quantum processors.
AI.method: Construct two-qubit quantum circuits using elements of the su(4) Cartan subalgebra. Each circuit applies the native gate twice and includes at least one CNOT gate. Six circuits measure entangling power (reducible to three with more CNOTs), and three circuits measure gate typicality.
AI.result: A set of six two-qubit circuits for entangling power measurement, reducible to three by increasing CNOT resources. A separate set of three circuits for gate typicality measurement, which requires more nonlocal resources than entangling power measurement.
AI.conclusion: These constructed circuits can determine the nonlocal characteristics of native gates in many quantum processors, with gate typicality measurement demanding more nonlocal resources than entangling power measurement.

title: VQCSim: When Does Compile-Once Statevector Simulation Beat Generic Quantum Frameworks?
comment: Accepted at IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026), San Jose, CA, USA. 9 pages
summary: Hybrid quantum-classical machine learning workflows repeatedly evaluate many small parametrized circuits during training and model exploration. In this regime, framework dispatch and orchestration overhead often dominate runtime. Prior simulators accelerate execution but leave open the question of when compile-once specialization is the right choice for static variational circuits. We answer this question with VQCSim, a compile-once, PyTorch-native statevector execution path with native autograd. In a systematic MQT Bench study, VQCSim compiles all tested static circuits and provides 87.7% end-to-end semantic validation. Across a five-GPU evaluation set, VQCSim delivers pooled median speedups of 4.49x for native inference and 26.78x for native training, while retaining a 3.31x advantage under matched finite-difference training. Ablation identifies native autograd as the dominant source of acceleration (27.6x), with compile-once caching and batch vectorization contributing additional gains. The speedup trades higher GPU memory (VQCSim is memory-limited at the high end) for lower runtime. We derive a hardware-aware regime map and release vqcsim-oracle, an open-source backend selector with 91.1%-97.7% top-1 agreement (including cross-GPU transfers), enabling automatic simulator selection in QML design loops.

AI.tldr: VQCSim is a compile-once, PyTorch-native statevector simulator for hybrid quantum-classical machine learning that delivers 4.49x inference and 26.78x training speedups via native autograd, with an open-source backend selector achieving 91.1%-97.7% top-1 agreement.
AI.motivation: Framework dispatch and orchestration overhead often dominate runtime in hybrid quantum-classical ML workflows that repeatedly evaluate many small parametrized circuits. The question of when compile-once specialization is the right choice for static variational circuits remained open.
AI.method: VQCSim implements a compile-once, PyTorch-native statevector execution path with native autograd. It performs systematic validation using MQT Bench (87.7% end-to-end semantic validation) and ablation studies to isolate contributions from native autograd, compile-once caching, and batch vectorization. A hardware-aware regime map and vqcsim-oracle backend selector are also developed.
AI.result: Pooled median speedups of 4.49x (inference) and 26.78x (training) across five GPUs; 3.31x advantage under matched finite-difference training. Native autograd is the dominant acceleration source (27.6x). The backend selector achieves 91.1%-97.7% top-1 agreement including cross-GPU transfers.
AI.conclusion: Compile-once specialization is the right choice for static variational circuits, and the trade-off of higher GPU memory for lower runtime is favorable. The released vqcsim-oracle enables automatic simulator selection in QML design loops.

title: Quantum-classical neurons upgraded with optical spin qubits for advanced computing and networking architectures
summary: Hardware neurons incorporating built-in memory components are critical technologies for implementing large scale neural networks that exhibit adaptive-itinerant behavior and produce biological-inspired spiking patterns that match neuroscience known operations (1). Moreover, neurons capable of full quantum information processing through their qubit states and quantum trajectory provides capability for hybrid quantum-classical operations through the level of coherence/entanglement and non-Markovianity (2,3). These attributes further contribute to solving complex quantum mechanical problems by providing a rich and diverse group for expressing quantum neural states. Upgrading these hardware neurons now with optical spin qubits excitable with pulsed laser excitation in the near infrared and designed from negatively charged silicon vacancies in semiconductor silicon carbide (4) and Neodymium rare earth ions in the superconducting Niobium/Niobium oxide film (5) that form the memory provides access to the unique spin Hamiltonian that considers electronic and nuclear interactions. In this manuscript, we experimentally measure opto-electronic quantum-classical neurons integrated with a optical spin qubit and examine how tailored neuronal spiking sequences drive the photoluminescence oscillations and modulate the quantum spin transitions. We derive a quantum model for the system that considers the interaction between the neuron and optical qubit spin and perform calculations to project how quantum computing operations are expandable across the state space in the quantum-classical neuron and spin qubit system. For example, the resulting impact on the neuron quantum states where the strength is adjustable due to dynamical memory changes. These results are critical for realizing hardware neurons with quantum optical capabilities and inspired by the existence in biology of biophotons.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally demonstrates opto-electronic quantum-classical neurons with optical spin qubits (silicon vacancies in SiC and Nd ions in Nb/NbO films), showing how spiking sequences modulate photoluminescence and spin transitions. A quantum model is derived for neuron-qubit interactions, projecting expandable quantum computing operations across the state space.
AI.motivation: Hardware neurons with built-in memory are critical for large-scale neural networks exhibiting adaptive-itinerant behavior and biological spiking patterns. Integrating quantum information processing via qubit states and quantum trajectories enables hybrid quantum-classical operations, solving complex quantum mechanical problems through rich quantum neural state representations.
AI.method: Experimental measurement of opto-electronic quantum-classical neurons integrated with optical spin qubits (negatively charged silicon vacancies in SiC and Neodymium rare earth ions in Nb/NbO films). Pulsed near-infrared laser excitation drives the spin qubits. Tailored neuronal spiking sequences drive photoluminescence oscillations and modulate quantum spin transitions. A quantum model is derived considering neuron-optical qubit spin interactions.
AI.result: Demonstration that spiking sequences modulate photoluminescence oscillations and quantum spin transitions. Calculations project how quantum computing operations are expandable across the state space, with neuron quantum state strength adjustable via dynamical memory changes.
AI.conclusion: These results are critical for realizing hardware neurons with quantum optical capabilities, inspired by biophotons in biology, enabling adaptive neural networks with full quantum information processing.

title: Remote Entanglement of Solid-State Spin Qubits Integrated in Broadband Waveguides
summary: Solid-state spin-photon interfaces promise to scale quantum networks through on-chip photonic integration and multiplexed entanglement generation. To date, remote entanglement between integrated emitters has been realized only in cavity-enhanced systems, where fabrication yield and spectral matching remain major obstacles. Here we demonstrate heralded remote entanglement between diamond tin-vacancy spin qubits embedded in separate on-chip waveguides. Combining intrinsically efficient photon emission with a broadband waveguide architecture provides high device yield and obviates the need for spectral matching to cavity modes. We realize coherent optical and spin control and achieve high-visibility two-photon interference. By combining photon-mediated entanglement generation with real-time feedforward, we produce a consistent entangled state independent of the heralding pattern. These results establish waveguide-integrated tin-vacancy centers as a compelling platform for scalable quantum network nodes.

AI.tldr: Demonstration of heralded remote entanglement between tin-vacancy spin qubits in separate on-chip waveguides, achieving high device yield without spectral matching to cavities.
AI.motivation: Overcoming fabrication yield and spectral matching obstacles in cavity-enhanced systems for scalable quantum networks.
AI.method: Using diamond tin-vacancy centers in broadband on-chip waveguides with intrinsically efficient photon emission, coherent optical/spin control, two-photon interference, and real-time feedforward for heralded entanglement.
AI.result: High-visibility two-photon interference and consistent entangled state generation independent of heralding pattern.
AI.conclusion: Waveguide-integrated tin-vacancy centers are a compelling platform for scalable quantum network nodes.

title: Quantum incompatibility of Born probabilities
summary: Quantum theory challenges the view that individual measurement outcomes are predefined and independent of the measurement context. Yet the quantum state itself -- the catalogue of probabilities for all possible measurements -- is usually assumed to be well defined. We argue that this assumption tacitly relies on measurements being performed relative to ideal, infinitely-resourceful reference frames. We show that, when measurements are made relative to non-ideal quantum reference frames, the probabilities themselves become indefinite: even in the limit of arbitrarily large number of runs, the relative frequencies may remain uncertain. The uncertainty is irreducible in a quantum-mechanical sense, as we show by proving a Bell-type theorem for relative frequencies. We further propose a quantum-optical implementation of these relational measurements based on pulsed homodyne detection. Our findings motivate an extension of the notion of the quantum state to regimes constrained by finite resources. We expect them to be especially relevant at the interface between quantum theory and general relativity, where the resources and information available in a bounded region of spacetime are fundamentally limited.

AI.tldr: Quantum states are not well-defined when measurements use non-ideal reference frames; probabilities become indefinite even in the infinite-run limit, as proven by a Bell-type theorem for relative frequencies.
AI.motivation: The assumption that quantum states are well-defined implicitly relies on ideal, infinitely-resourceful reference frames, which may not hold in resource-constrained regimes (e.g., at the interface of quantum theory and general relativity).
AI.method: The authors prove a Bell-type theorem for relative frequencies to demonstrate irreducible quantum uncertainty in measurement outcomes, and propose a quantum-optical implementation using pulsed homodyne detection.
AI.result: When measurements are made relative to non-ideal quantum reference frames, probabilities become indefinite and relative frequencies remain uncertain even in the limit of arbitrarily many runs; the uncertainty is irreducible in a quantum-mechanical sense.
AI.conclusion: The notion of the quantum state should be extended to account for finite-resource constraints, with particular relevance at the interface between quantum theory and general relativity where resources in bounded spacetime regions are fundamentally limited.

title: Quantum magic and non-commutativity as computational resources in quantum reservoir computing
summary: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) provides a hardware-efficient paradigm for temporal information processing on near-term quantum devices. Despite rapid experimental progress, a rigorous understanding of the structural conditions required for its scalable quantum-enhanced performance remains lacking. Here, we develop a theoretical framework in Pauli-Liouville space that provides a unified analytical treatment of the echo state property (ESP), nonlinear expressive power, and quantum resources. We first analyze the widely used qubit-resetting scheme and establish that quantum magic generated by reservoir dynamics is a necessary condition for effective computation, a requirement more fundamental than ESP. However, we prove that this architecture faces inherent expressivity limitations: all nonlinear processing originates exclusively from the classical encoding map, imposing an unavoidable trade-off between nonlinearity and memory capacity. To circumvent this structural bottleneck, we rigorously analyze Hamiltonian encoding, in which temporal inputs are embedded directly into the continuous dynamics generator. We show that the ESP is natively guaranteed by the Liouvillian spectral gap, decoupling it from quantum magic. Crucially, for any non-trivial drive Hamiltonian, the discrete-time update map exhibits a transcendental, infinite-order nonlinear dependence on the instantaneous input. Moreover, the intrinsic non-commutativity of the open-system generators governs the temporal coupling of these nonlinearities, producing highly non-separable processing of the input history. Our results establish a rigorous theoretical hierarchy of QRC architectures and provide prescriptive design principles for experiments targeting genuine quantum advantages in temporal processing.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a theoretical framework in Pauli-Liouville space to analyze quantum reservoir computing architectures, revealing fundamental limitations of qubit-resetting schemes (where nonlinearity comes only from classical encoding, creating a trade-off with memory) and showing that Hamiltonian encoding can overcome these limitations by providing infinite-order nonlinearity and non-separable temporal processing via non-commutative open-system generators.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous theoretical understanding of the structural conditions required for scalable quantum-enhanced performance in quantum reservoir computing, which currently lacks a unified analytical treatment of echo state property, nonlinear expressive power, and quantum resources.
AI.method: The authors develop a theoretical framework in Pauli-Liouville space that provides unified analytical treatment of ESP, nonlinear expressive power, and quantum resources. They analyze two architectures: qubit-resetting scheme and Hamiltonian encoding scheme.
AI.result: For qubit-resetting: quantum magic is necessary for computation but the architecture has inherent expressivity limitations — all nonlinear processing comes from classical encoding, creating an unavoidable nonlinearity-memory trade-off. For Hamiltonian encoding: ESP is guaranteed by Liouvillian spectral gap, decoupled from magic; the update map exhibits transcendental infinite-order nonlinearity; non-commutativity of generators governs temporal coupling of nonlinearities, enabling non-separable input history processing.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a rigorous theoretical hierarchy of QRC architectures and provide prescriptive design principles for experiments targeting genuine quantum advantages in temporal processing.

title: Dissipative phase transitions and chaos in two-photon driven quantum optomechanics
summary: We investigate nonequilibrium criticality and chaos in a two-photon-driven optomechanical system. The parametric drive preserves a discrete $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry of the optical field, while radiation-pressure coupling transfers the resulting nonlinear dynamics to a mechanical oscillator. Combining semiclassical stability analysis, exact Liouvillian spectra, and stochastic quantum trajectories, we show that this driven-dissipative optomechanical model supports both first- and second-order dissipative phase transitions. At negative detuning a second-order transition yields spontaneous breaking of the cavity-parity symmetry in the thermodynamic limit. At positive detuning the same symmetry breaking coexists with a first-order transition, signaled by metastability and by an additional symmetric Liouvillian mode. At stronger pump power the mean-field dynamics loses all stable fixed points and develops limit cycles and chaotic attractors with positive Lyapunov exponent. Quantum trajectories in this regime display chaotic-like motion, enhanced steady-state entropy, and delocalization over many entropic Liouvillian modes. These results establish two-photon-driven optomechanics as a platform where dissipative criticality, symmetry breaking, and quantum signatures of chaos emerge within the same experimentally accessible setting.

AI.tldr: This paper studies nonequilibrium criticality and chaos in a two-photon-driven optomechanical system, revealing both first- and second-order dissipative phase transitions, parity symmetry breaking, and quantum chaotic dynamics with limit cycles and positive Lyapunov exponents within a single platform.
AI.motivation: To explore how nonequilibrium criticality, symmetry breaking, and quantum chaos can coexist in a driven-dissipative optomechanical system with $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, providing a unified platform for studying these phenomena.
AI.method: Combination of semiclassical stability analysis, exact Liouvillian spectra computation, and stochastic quantum trajectory simulations to analyze the phase diagram and dynamics.
AI.result: At negative detuning, a second-order transition breaks cavity-parity symmetry. At positive detuning, first- and second-order transitions coexist with metastability. At strong pump power, the system develops limit cycles and chaotic attractors with positive Lyapunov exponents, and quantum trajectories show chaotic-like motion, enhanced entropy, and delocalization over many Liouvillian modes.
AI.conclusion: Two-photon-driven optomechanics serves as an experimentally accessible platform where dissipative phase transitions, symmetry breaking, and quantum signatures of chaos emerge together.

title: Observation of gravity-like signatures in holographic codes on a quantum computer
summary: The unification of quantum mechanics and general relativity remains one of the major open problems of theoretical physics. The Anti-de Sitter/Conformal Field Theory (AdS/CFT) correspondence provides a valuable theoretical framework for this effort via a holographic duality between a theory of quantum gravity in asymptotically AdS spacetime and a conformal quantum field theory on the lower-dimensional boundary. Here, we implement a toy model of this duality called the HaPPY code, a quantum error-correcting code in the form of a tensor network with hyperbolic entanglement patterns, on a trapped-ion quantum computer. We present the first experimental confirmation of the Faulkner-Lewkowycz-Maldacena formula in this model - a key test of the holographic correspondence. We then enrich it with non-stabilizerness, or magic, and observe entropic precursors expected of emergent gravity. Finally, we present and measure a code construction whose entropic behavior is reminiscent of a highly quantum wormhole. Our experiments illustrate how quantum computers can serve as testbeds for modeling the emergence of spacetime.

AI.tldr: The HaPPY code, a holographic quantum error-correcting code based on the AdS/CFT correspondence, was implemented on a trapped-ion quantum computer, experimentally confirming the Faulkner-Lewkowycz-Maldacena formula and demonstrating entropic signatures of emergent gravity and wormhole-like behavior through the addition of non-stabilizerness.
AI.motivation: Quantum gravity remains unresolved; the AdS/CFT correspondence offers a holographic framework linking quantum gravity in AdS spacetime to a conformal field theory on the boundary. The authors aim to experimentally test this duality using a tractable toy model on a quantum computer.
AI.method: Implemented the HaPPY code (a tensor network quantum error-correcting code with hyperbolic entanglement patterns) on a trapped-ion quantum computer. Enriched the model with non-stabilizerness (magic) and measured entropy behavior; also constructed and measured a code with entropic features resembling a quantum wormhole.
AI.result: First experimental confirmation of the Faulkner-Lewkowycz-Maldacena formula in the HaPPY code model. Observed entropic precursors of emergent gravity after introducing magic. Measured a code construction whose entropic behavior mimics a highly quantum wormhole.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computers can serve as experimental testbeds for modeling spacetime emergence and probing holographic dualities, providing evidence that tabletop quantum experiments can inform fundamental questions in quantum gravity.

title: Entangling Power and Symmetries in the Quantum Rabi Model
summary: The quantum Rabi model is a standard effective Hamiltonian in studies of light-matter interaction, capturing the simplest nontrivial setting in which a qubit couples to a single harmonic oscillator. Within the broader Rabi family, we focus on two special cases: the Jaynes-Cummings (JC) model, which carries an explicit $U(1)$ symmetry, and the asymmetric quantum Rabi model (AQRM), which possesses a parameter-dependent "hidden'' symmetry that appears only at integer bias, $\varepsilon/ω\in\mathbb{Z}$, and is not manifest in the Hamiltonian. We use the time-averaged entangling power as an operator-level diagnostic of these symmetry structures. Since the oscillator Hilbert space is infinite-dimensional, we compare two finite input ensembles: a Haar average after Fock-space truncation and a coherent-state average at fixed mean occupation $\bar{n}$. Both diagnostics show peaks at the integer-bias points of the AQRM, where the hidden symmetry resides. In contrast, the manifest $U(1)$ symmetry at the JC point instead gives a weak dip. Thus, the time-averaged entangling power responds to both the hidden symmetry and the $U(1)$ symmetry in the Rabi family, with the sign of the response indicating how the symmetry reorganizes the spectral expansion. These results demonstrate that the entangling power can serve as an operator diagnostic to reveal the presence and properties of hidden and manifest symmetries in light-matter systems.

AI.tldr: The paper uses time-averaged entangling power as an operator diagnostic to reveal hidden (integer-bias) and manifest (U(1) at JC point) symmetries in the quantum Rabi model family, showing peaks for hidden symmetry and dips for manifest symmetry.
AI.motivation: To develop an operator-level diagnostic for detecting hidden symmetries (such as the parameter-dependent symmetry in the asymmetric quantum Rabi model at integer bias) that are not manifest in the Hamiltonian, using entangling power as a probe.
AI.method: Compare two finite input ensembles: Haar average after Fock-space truncation and coherent-state average at fixed mean occupation $\bar{n}$, applied to the time-averaged entangling power of the Jaynes-Cummings model and the asymmetric quantum Rabi model.
AI.result: The entangling power exhibits peaks at integer-bias points (hidden symmetry) in the AQRM and a weak dip at the JC point (manifest $U(1)$ symmetry), showing opposite sign responses for hidden vs. manifest symmetries.
AI.conclusion: Time-averaged entangling power can serve as an effective operator diagnostic to reveal both hidden and manifest symmetries in light-matter systems, with the sign of the response indicating how the symmetry reorganizes the spectral expansion.

title: HarmQ: Harmonic Backdoor Attacks Against Quantum Neural Networks
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Accepted by the IEEE International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC 2026)
summary: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for quantum machine learning in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, leveraging quantum phenomena such as superposition and entanglement to process information in exponentially large Hilbert spaces. However, QNNs inherit critical security vulnerabilities from classical neural networks, particularly susceptibility to backdoor attacks. Existing attack methods designed for classical systems fail against QNNs due to quantum-specific constraints: aggressive downsampling required by limited qubit resources destroys conventional triggers, while the spectral learning bias of parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) restricts learnable patterns. To tackle this, we present HarmQ, a quantum-native backdoor attack that exploits PQCs' inherent Fourier decomposition bias through harmonic trigger patterns. Our approach employs sinusoidal perturbations on coarse grids with block-uniform structure, ensuring survival through downsampling while aligning with PQCs' preference for low-frequency components. This enables effective backdoor injection under realistic black-box conditions where attackers access only training data. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST demonstrate that HarmQ achieves attack success rates exceeding 99% while maintaining over 90% clean accuracy, significantly outperforming existing methods including BadNets (2.77% ASR), Watermark (7.96% ASR), Q-FGSM (44.32% ASR) and QUAP (3.40% ASR). Parametric t-SNE visualizations of quantum state representations confirm that harmonic triggers create distinctly separated clusters, evidencing HarmQ as a fundamental security threat for QNNs.

AI.tldr: HarmQ is a quantum-native backdoor attack that exploits the Fourier decomposition bias of parameterized quantum circuits by using harmonic sinusoidal perturbation patterns, achieving >99% attack success rate on QNNs while maintaining >90% clean accuracy.
AI.motivation: Quantum Neural Networks inherit critical security vulnerabilities from classical neural networks, particularly backdoor attacks, but existing classical attack methods fail against QNNs due to quantum-specific constraints like aggressive downsampling from limited qubit resources and the spectral learning bias of parameterized quantum circuits.
AI.method: HarmQ injects backdoors by employing sinusoidal perturbations on coarse grids with block-uniform structure (harmonic trigger patterns), which survive downsampling and align with PQCs' inherent Fourier decomposition bias toward low-frequency components, operating under realistic black-box conditions where attackers only access training data.
AI.result: On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, HarmQ achieves >99% attack success rate and >90% clean accuracy, significantly outperforming BadNets (2.77% ASR), Watermark (7.96% ASR), Q-FGSM (44.32% ASR), and QUAP (3.40% ASR). Parametric t-SNE visualizations confirm harmonic triggers create distinctly separated clusters in quantum state representations.
AI.conclusion: HarmQ demonstrates that quantum-native backdoor attacks exploiting PQCs' spectral biases pose a fundamental security threat to QNNs, and the successful creation of distinctly separated quantum state clusters evidences the effectiveness of this attack paradigm.

title: Molecular Docking with Quantum Circuit Evolution
summary: Molecular docking is an important step in drug discovery, enabling the evaluation of receptor-ligand affinity while reducing experimental costs and increasing the number of possible tests. However, the high computational cost associated with molecular docking remains a limiting factor that can restrict both the experimental precision and the scale of the problems being addressed. To improve the future applicability of molecular docking, recent works have proposed the use of quantum algorithms based on Gaussian Boson Sampling quantum computers and also gate-based quantum computers. In this work, we propose the use of Quantum Circuit Evolution (QCE) for solving the molecular docking problem, a gate based and gradient-free quantum evolutionary method whose evolution is driven by the random application of unitary operations to a quantum circuit. The proposed algorithm demonstrated the ability to find the best solution to the problem in fewer steps than the methods presented in previous studies, exhibiting fast and stable convergence.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Quantum Circuit Evolution (QCE), a gate-based, gradient-free quantum evolutionary method for molecular docking that achieves faster and more stable convergence to optimal solutions than prior quantum approaches.
AI.motivation: Molecular docking is computationally expensive, limiting precision and scalability in drug discovery. Existing quantum approaches (Gaussian Boson Sampling and gate-based methods) still face efficiency issues.
AI.method: Quantum Circuit Evolution (QCE) — a gate-based, gradient-free quantum evolutionary algorithm where evolution is driven by random application of unitary operations to a quantum circuit.
AI.result: The QCE algorithm finds the best solution in fewer steps than prior methods, exhibiting fast and stable convergence.
AI.conclusion: QCE outperforms previous quantum docking approaches in convergence speed and stability, improving the practical applicability of quantum computing for molecular docking.

title: Defeating Barren Plateaus with Task-Aligned Symmetry
summary: Barren plateaus -- the exponential vanishing of gradients -- are a fundamental obstacle to training scalable quantum neural networks. Whether they arise in quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs), a natural architecture for sequential data, remains a pressing question. Here we show that the decisive ingredient for trainability in QRNNs is not the recurrent circuit topology per se, but enforcing time-translation symmetry through parameter sharing across time steps. We prove that, without parameter sharing, QRNNs suffer from barren plateaus, with gradient variance decaying exponentially with sequence length. Imposing parameter sharing across time steps fundamentally alters this scaling, transforming it into a polynomial dependence and thereby suppressing the barren plateau. Numerical simulations corroborate these analytical predictions. By rigorously showing how time-translation symmetry suppresses barren plateaus and enhances learning capability in QRNNs, our work establishes task-aligned symmetry as a constructive resolution to the expressivity-trainability tension in quantum neural networks.

AI.tldr: Barren plateaus in quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) are caused not by recurrent topology but by lack of time-translation symmetry. Parameter sharing across time steps suppresses barren plateaus, changing gradient variance scaling from exponential to polynomial with sequence length.
AI.motivation: Barren plateaus (exponential vanishing of gradients) are a fundamental obstacle to scaling quantum neural networks, and whether they arise in QRNNs — a natural architecture for sequential data — was an open pressing question.
AI.method: The authors analytically derive gradient variance scaling for QRNNs with and without parameter sharing across time steps, and validate predictions with numerical simulations.
AI.result: Without parameter sharing, QRNNs suffer barren plateaus with gradient variance decaying exponentially with sequence length. Imposing parameter sharing (time-translation symmetry) changes this to polynomial dependence, suppressing the barren plateau.
AI.conclusion: Task-aligned symmetry (time-translation) constructively resolves the expressivity-trainability tension in quantum neural networks by suppressing barren plateaus while preserving learning capability.

title: Error correction on an array of superconducting qubits with defective components
comment: 11 pages + 5 page appendix, 10 figures, comments welcome
summary: A solid-state quantum-computing architecture will require the fabrication of arrays of many coupled qubits. It is inevitable that this process will produce qubits and couplers with varying performance, with some components underperforming due to imperfect fabrication. Quantum error-correction requires high-performing components and hence these defects must be dealt with, either by adapting the code to exclude the defects, or by informing the decoder to accommodate defects in post-processing. Here we implement and compare strategies to operate distance-5 surface codes on a quantum processor consisting of a square-lattice array of 120 superconducting qubits. We demonstrate a dramatic reduction in the probability of a logical error in a memory experiment by excluding underperforming components, compared with both a standard approach of ignoring defects, and a defect-aware decoding approach. We observe up to 2.8X improvement in logical errors per round when excluding defects compared with the standard defect-ignorant approach (1.62% compared to 4.49%). In contrast, defect-aware decoding gives only modest gains. Defects are also expected to be particularly harmful for measurement-based logical operations. Using a stability experiment we show that excluding defects resurrects measurement-based logic gate performance, observing a 6.3% per-round suppression of failure rate when excluding defects, compared to zero suppression otherwise. Furthermore, we show a further substantial decrease in logical errors when using leakage post-selection in combination with our defect exclusion strategies, resulting in a distance-5 code outperforming the best distance-3 in one basis. Our experiments therefore give a proof-of-principle demonstration of the essential utility of defect exclusion methods in the scale-up of solid-state quantum computing approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that excluding underperforming qubits and couplers in a 120-superconducting-qubit surface code processor dramatically reduces logical errors (up to 2.8× improvement) compared to standard defect-ignorant or defect-aware decoding approaches, and also resurrects measurement-based logic gate performance. Combining defect exclusion with leakage post-selection yields further improvements, enabling a distance-5 code to outperform a distance-3 code in one basis.
AI.motivation: Solid-state quantum computing requires large arrays of coupled qubits, but inevitable fabrication imperfections produce underperforming components. Quantum error correction demands high-performing components, so strategies must be developed to handle these defects—either by adapting the code to exclude defects or by informing the decoder.
AI.method: The authors implement and compare three strategies—defect-ignorant (standard), defect-aware decoding, and defect exclusion—on a square-lattice array of 120 superconducting qubits running distance-5 surface codes. They evaluate logical error rates in memory experiments and failure rates in stability experiments (measurement-based logic gates), also combining defect exclusion with leakage post-selection.
AI.result: Defect exclusion yields up to 2.8× improvement in logical errors per round (1.62% vs 4.49% for defect-ignorant). Defect-aware decoding shows only modest gains. In stability experiments, defect exclusion gives 6.3% per-round suppression of failure rate versus zero suppression otherwise. Combining defect exclusion with leakage post-selection enables a distance-5 code to outperform the best distance-3 code in one basis.
AI.conclusion: Defect exclusion methods are essential for scaling up solid-state quantum computing approaches, providing a proof-of-principle demonstration of their utility in improving logical error performance and enabling measurement-based logical operations.

title: Categorical Tensor-Graph Semantics for Quantum Algorithms
summary: This paper systematically investigates quantum computing protocols from the intuitive perspective of categorical tensor-graph semantics within the category FHilb. While conventional Hilbert-space formalisms conceal the structural nature of quantum algorithms behind high-dimensional matrix operations, the topological framework developed herein directly encodes algorithmic functionalities to their graphical skeletons. We provide a comprehensive topological reinterpretation of the Bernstein-Vazirani and the Simon algorithms, demonstrating how topological transformations distill their core mathematical essence and clarify the operational mechanism of oracles. Going beyond standard qubit models, we formalize the qutrit-adapted generalized Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm as well as the generalized single-shot Grover algorithm, explicitly laying out their graphical representations. We further implement CNOT gates via complementary Frobenius structures, trace the diagrammatic genesis of quantum entanglement including Bell and GHZ states, and present a diagrammatic simplification for W-state preparation protocol. By bridging tensor category theory with practical quantum algorithmic design, this work furnishes composable, scalable diagrammatic toolkit essential for automated circuit optimization across the evolving quantum hardware ecosystem.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a categorical tensor-graph semantics within the category FHilb to reinterpret quantum algorithms (Bernstein-Vazirani, Simon, Deutsch-Jozsa, Grover) topologically, implements CNOT via Frobenius structures, and provides diagrammatic simplifications for entanglement states (Bell, GHZ, W-state), aiming at composable and scalable circuit optimization.
AI.motivation: Conventional Hilbert-space formalisms obscure the structural nature of quantum algorithms behind high-dimensional matrix operations, motivating a topological framework that directly encodes algorithmic functionalities into graphical skeletons.
AI.method: The paper employs categorical tensor-graph semantics within FHilb, using topological transformations to distill algorithmic essence, formalizing qutrit-adapted Deutsch-Jozsa and generalized single-shot Grover algorithms via graphical representations, and implementing CNOT gates through complementary Frobenius structures.
AI.result: Provides comprehensive topological reinterpretations of Bernstein-Vazirani, Simon, Deutsch-Jozsa, and Grover algorithms; delivers diagrammatic simplifications for Bell, GHZ, and W-state preparation; and establishes a composable diagrammatic toolkit for automated circuit optimization.
AI.conclusion: Bridging tensor category theory with practical quantum algorithmic design yields a scalable, composable diagrammatic framework suitable for automated optimization across evolving quantum hardware ecosystems.

title: Witnessing the Quantum Mpemba Effect with a Single Observable
summary: The Mpemba effect, in which a system farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one closer to it, defies the intuition of nonequilibrium statistical mechanics. Here, we introduce a general framework to unambiguously witness this phenomenon based on a single observable defined for Markovian open quantum systems. The Mpemba observable bypasses full state tomography, offering utility for state preparation and thermal task optimization. We illustrate our method using local magnetization as a Mpemba signature, applying it to a qubit under generalized amplitude damping.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a general framework to witness the Mpemba effect in Markovian open quantum systems using a single observable (the Mpemba observable), which bypasses full state tomography and is demonstrated on a qubit under generalized amplitude damping using local magnetization.
AI.motivation: The Mpemba effect defies intuition in nonequilibrium statistical mechanics; a general framework to unambiguously witness this phenomenon is needed.
AI.method: The authors introduce a general framework based on a single observable (the Mpemba observable) defined for Markovian open quantum systems, which bypasses full state tomography.
AI.result: The framework is illustrated using local magnetization as a Mpemba signature, applied to a qubit under generalized amplitude damping.
AI.conclusion: The Mpemba observable offers utility for state preparation and thermal task optimization.

title: Axion like particles multi-parameter sensing
summary: The search for the axion like particles (APLs)-one of the deepest puzzles in modern cosmology-may hold the key to understanding dark matter and dark energy. In this work, we introduce a setup taking advantage of the quantum metrology techniques to constrain the hypothetical mass and coupling constants of APLs by employing exotic pseudoscalar spin-spin interactions between fermions mediated by ALPs. A key advantage of our approach is the exploitation of position-dependent spin sensor results to the high sensitivity of the probe. To simultaneously investigate the axion mass and coupling constants, we invoke a multi-probe detection strategy. Through this strategy, we circumvent the singularity of the quantum Fisher information matrix as an ultimate upper bound on the sensitivity of any probe. For the axion masses in the range of $m_a {\le} 10^{-3} \text{eV}$, this setup can exclude values of axion coupling constants $g^e_pg^n_p$ down to $10^{-7}$.

AI.tldr: A quantum metrology setup using exotic spin-spin interactions to constrain axion-like particle (ALP) parameters, achieving coupling constant sensitivity down to 10⁻⁷ for axion masses ≤ 10⁻³ eV via a multi-probe strategy that avoids quantum Fisher information matrix singularities.
AI.motivation: The search for axion-like particles (ALPs) is a deep puzzle in modern cosmology, potentially key to understanding dark matter and dark energy. The authors aim to constrain the hypothetical mass and coupling constants of ALPs using quantum metrology techniques.
AI.method: The setup exploits exotic pseudoscalar spin-spin interactions between fermions mediated by ALPs, using position-dependent spin sensors for high sensitivity. A multi-probe detection strategy is employed to circumvent the singularity of the quantum Fisher information matrix, enabling simultaneous investigation of axion mass and coupling constants.
AI.result: For axion masses m_a ≤ 10⁻³ eV, the setup can exclude axion coupling constants g_p^e g_p^n down to 10⁻⁷.
AI.conclusion: The quantum metrology-based multi-probe approach effectively constrains ALP parameters, overcoming the quantum Fisher information matrix singularity, and achieves competitive exclusion limits on coupling constants in the low-mass regime.

title: Anticipating Decoder Side-channel Attacks in Fault-tolerant Quantum Computers
summary: As quantum computing emerges as an applied technology, there is a growing need to protect quantum computers against information security attacks. This work identifies a new class of side-channel attacks against fault-tolerant quantum computers, in which the syndrome data that is sent to the decoder system is used to infer which computation (logical circuit) is taking place on the quantum computer. Our work introduces the concept of gate fingerprints, which describes those patterns present in syndrome data that indicate which logical operation took place on the quantum computer. We show different effects by which logical operations produce gate fingerprints by focusing on Clifford+T computation in the surface code. We then explore how gate fingerprint information can be used to make inferences about the circuits or algorithms run on a quantum computer. Our findings indicate that decoder systems can be a vector for side-channel attacks and thus to prevent this, decoder systems should either be secured or built by a trusted party.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a new class of side-channel attacks against fault-tolerant quantum computers, where syndrome data sent to the decoder system reveals which logical circuit is being executed via "gate fingerprints" in the surface code, indicating that decoder systems must be secured or built by trusted parties.
AI.motivation: As quantum computing becomes an applied technology, there is a growing need to protect quantum computers against information security attacks, specifically side-channel attacks that exploit syndrome data in the decoding process.
AI.method: The authors introduce the concept of "gate fingerprints"—patterns present in syndrome data that indicate which logical operation took place. They analyze Clifford+T computation in the surface code to demonstrate how logical operations produce distinguishable gate fingerprints.
AI.result: Gate fingerprint information can be used to make inferences about the circuits or algorithms run on a quantum computer, showing that decoder systems can serve as a vector for side-channel attacks.
AI.conclusion: To prevent such side-channel attacks, decoder systems should either be secured or built by a trusted party.

title: Nearly optimal polynomial approximations for the quantum singular value transform
summary: We introduce polynomial approximations of the even and odd step functions on the interval $[-1,1]$ with simple Chebyshev coefficients, making their numerical implementation straightforward. We derive rigorous error bounds and demonstrate that these polynomials are nearly optimal in the sense that their error deviates from the theoretically optimal error by a multiplicative factor that grows logarithmically with the polynomial order. From these polynomials, we derive related nearly optimal polynomial approximations that can be used to perform quantum phase estimation, linear amplitude amplification, eigenvalue thresholding, and other quantum algorithms using the quantum singular value transform.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces polynomial approximations of even and odd step functions using simple Chebyshev coefficients with rigorous error bounds. These are nearly optimal (error deviates from optimal by a logarithmic factor) and are applied to quantum algorithms like phase estimation, amplitude amplification, eigenvalue thresholding, and quantum singular value transform.
AI.motivation: To develop practical, nearly optimal polynomial approximations of step functions that are easy to implement numerically and can be used to improve quantum algorithms such as quantum phase estimation, linear amplitude amplification, and eigenvalue thresholding.
AI.method: The authors construct polynomial approximations of even and odd step functions on $[-1,1]$ using simple Chebyshev coefficients, derive rigorous error bounds, and show the error is nearly optimal (multiplicative factor logarithmic in polynomial order). These approximations are then applied to quantum algorithms via the quantum singular value transform.
AI.result: The polynomial approximations are nearly optimal, with error deviating from the theoretically optimal error by a factor that grows logarithmically with polynomial order. They enable practical implementations of quantum phase estimation, linear amplitude amplification, eigenvalue thresholding, and other algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The presented Chebyshev-based polynomial step function approximations offer a numerically simple, nearly optimal approach for implementing several key quantum algorithms, bridging theory and practical numerical implementation.

title: Constant-Depth Multi-Product Formula for Trotter Error Mitigation in Near-Term Digital Quantum Simulation
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 1 table; with Supplementary Material (6 pages, 5 figures)
summary: Digital quantum simulation of many-body dynamics faces a tension between algorithmic Trotter error and physical noise that accumulates with circuit depth. Typical higher-order product formulas mitigate the algorithmic error at the cost of deeper circuits. Our benchmark shows that, within the limited physical error budget, the feasible advantage is confined to absolute errors well below the $10^{-2}$ scale, which vanishes under noise levels of current quantum hardware. In sharp contrast to the previous Trotter error mitigation methods, we introduce a constant-depth multi-product formula (cd-MPF) that suppresses the Trotter error by combining multiple circuits at fixed circuit depth. We identify an auxiliary parameter $α$, which reshapes the Trotter error terms while leaving the target evolution invariant. The classical linear combination of the measured expectation values cancels the leading $(Δt)^{2}$ algorithmic contribution and steepens the Trotter-error scaling with the two-qubit circuit depth $d$ from $d^{-2}$ to $d^{-4}$. Combined with physical-noise mitigation, our method can serve as a key ingredient for realizing long-time quantum dynamics simulation on near-term hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a constant-depth multi-product formula (cd-MPF) that suppresses Trotter error in quantum simulation by combining multiple fixed-depth circuits, achieving steeper error scaling (from d^{-2} to d^{-4}) without increasing circuit depth, unlike traditional higher-order product formulas that trade depth for accuracy.
AI.motivation: Digital quantum simulation of many-body dynamics faces a trade-off between algorithmic Trotter error and physical noise that accumulates with circuit depth. Higher-order product formulas reduce algorithmic error but require deeper circuits, which are impractical under current hardware noise levels.
AI.method: The authors propose a constant-depth multi-product formula (cd-MPF) that combines multiple circuits at fixed depth. An auxiliary parameter α reshapes Trotter error terms while preserving the target evolution. Classical post-processing linearly combines measured expectation values to cancel the leading (Δt)² algorithmic contribution.
AI.result: The method steepens Trotter-error scaling with two-qubit circuit depth d from d^{-2} to d^{-4}. Traditional higher-order formulas show feasible advantage only for absolute errors below 10^{-2}, which vanishes under current hardware noise.
AI.conclusion: Combined with physical-noise mitigation, cd-MPF can serve as a key ingredient for realizing long-time quantum dynamics simulation on near-term hardware.

title: Nonequilibrium thermodynamics of the acoustoelectric quantum vacuum
summary: The quantum vacuum can assume thermal properties as a consequence of system kinematics, highlighting the nuance of our definition of particles in quantum field theory. Here, we explore this phenomenon in acoustoelectric systems, involving the interaction of phonons and plasmons, where the charge carriers drift at a constant velocity exceeding the speed of sound. Through an open quantum systems analysis, we show that the acoustoelectric quantum vacuum acquires a thermal character with a temperature defined by the drift velocity and the phonon wavevector. Realistic parameters yield effective temperatures of several Kelvin, establishing acoustoelectric systems as a promising platform for the investigation of quantum vacuum effects.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that the quantum vacuum in acoustoelectric systems (where charge carriers drift faster than sound) acquires thermal properties with an effective temperature of several Kelvin, making these systems a promising platform for studying quantum vacuum effects.
AI.motivation: To explore the thermal properties of the quantum vacuum in acoustoelectric systems, where charge carrier drift velocity exceeds the speed of sound, and to establish such systems as a viable platform for investigating quantum vacuum phenomena.
AI.method: Open quantum systems analysis of acoustoelectric systems involving phonon-plasmon interactions with supersonic charge carrier drift.
AI.result: The acoustoelectric quantum vacuum acquires a thermal character with a temperature determined by drift velocity and phonon wavevector; realistic parameters produce effective temperatures of several Kelvin.
AI.conclusion: Acoustoelectric systems are a promising platform for investigating quantum vacuum effects, as they can exhibit measurable thermal vacuum properties at several Kelvin.

title: A fault-tolerant quantum blockchain deployed on commercial telecommunications network
summary: Popularized by the Bitcoin cryptocurrency, blockchain technology establishes a decentralized digital framework that utilizes cryptographic and consensus protocols to secure data against unauthorized modification. Consequently, blockchain has found broad adoption across diverse fields, including finance, data management, healthcare, and digital asset governance. In the quantum computing era, a paramount objective for blockchain is to preserve its foundational advantages of cryptographic integrity and decentralized fault-tolerant resilience. In principle, quantum digital signatures and quantum Byzantine agreement protocols offer foundational security guarantees and tolerate up to one-half of malicious nodes for blockchain. However, the practical realization of such a quantum-enhanced blockchain remains a significant and multifaceted challenge. Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a fully operational hybrid quantum blockchain architecture built on photonic integrated circuits and deployed over commercially available classical telecommunications infrastructure. The system achieves a fault tolerance of nearly one-half, surpassing the classical limit, while reaching consensus on a timescale of seconds. A deployed food traceability application validates the practicality of the proposed architecture, achieving a throughput of approximately 500 transactions per second. This work establishes a foundation for practical quantum blockchains, enabling secure, scalable, and decentralized information processing in the emerging quantum era.

AI.tldr: A hybrid quantum blockchain architecture built on photonic integrated circuits is proposed and experimentally demonstrated, achieving fault tolerance nearly one-half (surpassing classical limit), consensus in seconds, and ~500 transactions per second throughput in a food traceability application.
AI.motivation: To preserve blockchain's cryptographic integrity and decentralized fault-tolerant resilience in the quantum computing era by practically realizing a quantum-enhanced blockchain using quantum digital signatures and quantum Byzantine agreement.
AI.method: Hybrid quantum blockchain architecture built on photonic integrated circuits, deployed over commercially available classical telecommunications infrastructure, utilizing quantum digital signatures and quantum Byzantine agreement protocols.
AI.result: Achieves fault tolerance of nearly one-half (surpassing classical Byzantine limit), consensus on a timescale of seconds, and approximately 500 transactions per second throughput in a food traceability application.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a foundation for practical quantum blockchains, enabling secure, scalable, and decentralized information processing in the emerging quantum era.

title: Experimental demonstration of scalable quantum blockchain with exponentially superior quantum communication complexity
summary: To secure modern distributed digital infrastructures, quantum blockchains exploit quantum resources to achieve information-theoretic security and surpass the classical one-third fault-tolerance bound. However, existing high-fault-tolerant protocols face a fundamental scalability challenge: the blockchain trilemma imposes either exponential communication complexity or experimentally demanding multipartite entanglement. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a scalable quantum blockchain protocol based on weak coherent states that achieves an exponential reduction in quantum communication complexity. The protocol employs a circular quantum Byzantine agreement mechanism that preserves information-theoretic security while avoiding multipartite entanglement. We implement this protocol on a photonic integrated circuit platform, realizing a six-node network over commercially available telecommunication infrastructure. Compared with previous schemes, the protocol requires less than 4% of the quantum communication resources. Leveraging this advantage, we further demonstrate a quantum-secured token exchange application achieving a throughput of 805.3 transactions per second with zero failures. These results establish a practical pathway toward scalable quantum blockchain.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates a scalable quantum blockchain protocol using weak coherent states on a photonic integrated circuit, achieving exponential reduction in quantum communication complexity, requiring less than 4% of previous quantum resources, and demonstrating a quantum-secured token exchange with 805.3 transactions per second and zero failures.
AI.motivation: Existing high-fault-tolerant quantum blockchain protocols face a scalability challenge due to the blockchain trilemma, which imposes either exponential communication complexity or experimentally demanding multipartite entanglement, hindering practical deployment.
AI.method: The protocol employs weak coherent states and a circular quantum Byzantine agreement mechanism that preserves information-theoretic security while avoiding multipartite entanglement. It is implemented on a photonic integrated circuit platform, realizing a six-node network over commercially available telecommunication infrastructure.
AI.result: The protocol achieves an exponential reduction in quantum communication complexity, requiring less than 4% of the quantum communication resources compared to previous schemes. A quantum-secured token exchange application achieves 805.3 transactions per second with zero failures.
AI.conclusion: These results establish a practical pathway toward scalable quantum blockchain, overcoming the fundamental scalability limitations of previous approaches.

title: Heisenberg Scaling in Many-Body Kinetic Uncertainty Relation via Quantum Feedback
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures; 9 pages of supplementary material
summary: Precision is a central figure of merit for quantum devices, including quantum clocks whose performance is determined by the stability of counting events. Kinetic uncertainty relations set fundamental limits on the precision of such counting observables, showing that their fluctuations cannot be suppressed without increasing the activity of the system. While many-body effects offer a natural route to enhanced performance, it remains unclear how far they can enhance counting precision. In quantum metrology, Heisenberg scaling refers to the suppression of estimation variance as $1/N^2$ with the particle number $N$. This raises the question of whether the fluctuation of counting observables can exhibit an analogous Heisenberg-like $1/N^2$ scaling, but no protocol for achieving it has been established. We establish a protocol that achieves this scaling by applying quantum feedback to a superradiant spin ensemble. Because the superradiant enhancement of activity is transient, the scaling of counting precision becomes achievable only when it is controlled by feedback. We establish this result analytically through a many-body kinetic uncertainty relation and feedback-modified mean-field equations, and show it by numerical simulations. Our results demonstrate that feedback can turn collective dissipation into a resource for Heisenberg scaling of counting precision.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that quantum feedback applied to a superradiant spin ensemble can achieve Heisenberg-like $1/N^2$ scaling for counting precision, overcoming the limitations imposed by kinetic uncertainty relations through feedback-controlled collective dissipation.
AI.motivation: Kinetic uncertainty relations set fundamental limits on counting precision, and it was unclear whether many-body effects could achieve Heisenberg scaling ($1/N^2$) for counting observables analogous to quantum metrology. No protocol for achieving such scaling had been established.
AI.method: The authors employ quantum feedback control on a superradiant spin ensemble, using a many-body kinetic uncertainty relation and feedback-modified mean-field equations for analytical derivation, complemented by numerical simulations.
AI.result: The protocol achieves Heisenberg-like $1/N^2$ scaling of counting precision by using feedback to sustain superradiant enhancement of activity, which is otherwise transient. Feedback turns collective dissipation into a resource for enhanced precision.
AI.conclusion: Quantum feedback can transform collective dissipation into a resource, enabling Heisenberg scaling of counting precision in many-body quantum systems, thereby establishing a fundamental connection between feedback control and quantum metrological scaling.

title: Demonstration of tripartite cat states in two distinct classes of entanglement
