comment: Main text: 7 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary information: 18 pages, 9 figures
summary: Entanglement is a cornerstone of quantum mechanics and an essential resource for quantum computation, communication, and metrology. While bipartite entanglement is extensively studied, genuine multipartite entangled states remain largely inaccessible in the macroscopic continuous-variable domain. Here, we experimentally realize macroscopic tripartite entangled cat states of the two distinct classes with fundamentally inequivalent properties, namely GHZ-cat and W-cat states, encoded across three microwave resonators coupled to an ancillary superconducting transmon. We develop one-to-all conditional controls on the three oscillators by fully utilizing three energy levels of the transmon to generate these states in a single piece of hardware and employ an efficient subspace tomography protocol for state reconstruction. We obtain GHZ-cat and W-cat states with fidelities $0.83\pm0.02$ and $0.70\pm0.02$, respectively, certifying genuine multipartite entanglement among the three oscillators. We further validate the distinct entanglement classes by experimentally demonstrating that pairwise entanglement is present in the W-cat state but absent in the GHZ-cat state. Our technique for the on-demand generation and characterization of inequivalent classes of tripartite continuous-variable entanglement provides a valuable testbed for future studies of macroscopic many-body entanglement and fault-tolerant quantum information processing with multipartite bosonic codes.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally realizes macroscopic tripartite entangled cat states (GHZ-cat and W-cat) across three microwave resonators using a single superconducting transmon, achieving fidelities of 0.83 and 0.70, and certifying genuine multipartite continuous-variable entanglement with distinct inequivalent properties.
AI.motivation: While bipartite entanglement is well-studied, genuine multipartite entangled states in the macroscopic continuous-variable domain remain largely inaccessible, motivating the need for their experimental realization and characterization.
AI.method: The authors use one-to-all conditional controls on three microwave resonators via three energy levels of an ancillary superconducting transmon, employing an efficient subspace tomography protocol for state reconstruction.
AI.result: GHZ-cat and W-cat states are produced with fidelities 0.83±0.02 and 0.70±0.02, certifying genuine multipartite entanglement. Pairwise entanglement is present in W-cat but absent in GHZ-cat, validating distinct entanglement classes.
AI.conclusion: The on-demand generation and characterization of inequivalent tripartite continuous-variable entanglement provides a testbed for macroscopic many-body entanglement and fault-tolerant quantum information processing with multipartite bosonic codes.

title: Parallel Hadamard Test
summary: The Hadamard test is a fundamental building block widely used in many quantum computing algorithms. It estimates the real or imaginary part of $\langle ψ\vert U \vert ψ\rangle$, where $\vert ψ\rangle$ is a quantum state and $U$ is a unitary operator. In many algorithms, however, many such quantities must be estimated, leading to a large number of distinct circuit types, long computational times, and high financial costs. In this work, we propose the parallel Hadamard test, which combines multiple Hadamard tests into a single circuit type. We demonstrate how the parallel Hadamard test applies to three structural classes of workloads: arbitrary sets of unitary operators, prefix-product arrays, and Gram-matrix elements. For each class, we compare the cost of the parallel Hadamard test with that of the conventional one. Our unified approach significantly reduces the number of distinct circuit types, and can lower both computational time and financial costs in regimes where fixed per-circuit overheads dominate the total cost. In Gram-matrix workloads, it can also reduce the total number of shots when typical off-diagonal overlaps are small.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a parallel Hadamard test that combines multiple Hadamard tests into a single circuit type, reducing circuit diversity, computational time, and financial costs for three workload classes: arbitrary unitary sets, prefix-product arrays, and Gram-matrix elements.
AI.motivation: In many quantum algorithms, numerous quantities of the form ⟨ψ|U|ψ⟩ must be estimated via the Hadamard test, leading to many distinct circuit types, long computational times, and high financial costs.
AI.method: The parallel Hadamard test combines multiple Hadamard tests into a single circuit type. The authors demonstrate its application to three workload classes: arbitrary unitary operator sets, prefix-product arrays, and Gram-matrix elements, and compare costs against the conventional approach.
AI.result: The parallel Hadamard test significantly reduces the number of distinct circuit types, lowers computational time and financial costs when fixed per-circuit overheads dominate, and for Gram-matrix workloads can also reduce total shot count when off-diagonal overlaps are small.
AI.conclusion: The unified parallel Hadamard test offers a more efficient alternative to conventional Hadamard tests by consolidating multiple estimations into a single circuit type, with benefits in circuit diversity reduction, computational time, and financial cost, especially under fixed overhead-dominated regimes or small off-diagonal overlaps in Gram-matrix settings.

title: Deterministic Minimum-Leakage Continuous-Variable Quantum Key Distribution with Phase-Conjugated Twin Beams
summary: Minimum-leakage continuous-variable quantum key distribution suppresses Eve's Holevo information by engineering the signal ensemble at the state-preparation stage. Existing symmetric minimum-leakage protocols achieve this goal by heralding: Alice interferes two squeezed ensembles, measures one output mode, and sends the other to Bob. Here we propose a deterministic two-mode protocol that removes the Alice-side heralding step. Alice combines two oppositely squeezed Gaussian ensembles on a balanced beam splitter and transmits both output modes, which form phase-conjugated twin beams. We show that this protocol is related to the heralding protocol through a common entanglement-based source but corresponds to a different prepare-and-measure decomposition. In the very-large-squeezing limit, the two protocols give the same secret key rate per transmitted optical mode. For finite squeezing, however, the phase-conjugated twin-beam protocol requires approximately 3 dB less squeezing to achieve the same key rate. We further analyze correlated two-mode Gaussian attacks in which Eve injects ancillary modes with optimized inter-mode correlations. We find that the correlated attacks are slightly more efficient than independent attacks, but the advantage remains limited under the minimum-leakage condition. These results show that phase-conjugated twin beams provide a deterministic and experimentally appealing route to symmetric minimum-leakage CV-QKD.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a deterministic two-mode continuous-variable QKD protocol using phase-conjugated twin beams that removes the heralding step of existing symmetric minimum-leakage protocols, achieving comparable performance with ~3 dB less squeezing requirement, while showing correlated two-mode Gaussian attacks provide only limited advantage under the minimum-leakage condition.
AI.motivation: To develop a deterministic (non-heralding) symmetric minimum-leakage CV-QKD protocol that is experimentally simpler while maintaining security and performance, and to analyze its resilience against correlated two-mode Gaussian attacks.
AI.method: The authors propose a phase-conjugated twin-beam protocol where Alice combines two oppositely squeezed Gaussian ensembles on a balanced beam splitter and transmits both output modes, eliminating the heralding step. They relate this to the existing heralding protocol through a common entanglement-based source but with a different prepare-and-measure decomposition, and analyze security against correlated two-mode Gaussian attacks.
AI.result: In the very-large-squeezing limit, both protocols achieve the same secret key rate per transmitted mode. For finite squeezing, the phase-conjugated twin-beam protocol requires ~3 dB less squeezing for the same key rate. Correlated two-mode Gaussian attacks are slightly more efficient than independent attacks, but their advantage is limited under minimum-leakage conditions.
AI.conclusion: Phase-conjugated twin beams provide a deterministic and experimentally appealing route to symmetric minimum-leakage CV-QKD, offering improved squeezing efficiency while maintaining security against correlated attacks.

title: Q2NSViz: An Open-source Standalone Visualizer for Quantum Network Simulations
comment: This work has been funded by the European Union under Horizon Europe ERC-CoG grant QNattyNet ("Quantum-Native Communication Networks: from Quantum Message to Quantum Functioning"), n.101169850. Details at https://qnattynet.quantuminternet.it
summary: The unique and non-classical features of quantum networks make their simulation and intuitive understanding inherently difficult. In this work, we present Q2NSViz, an open-source Python-based visualization tool for replaying and inspecting quantum-network simulation traces. Q2NSViz reconstructs the time evolution of the simulated network state, including physical topology, stored and in-flight qubits, classical bits and packets, measurements, and entanglement relationships. In this way, it exposes not only physical connectivity, but also the dynamic entanglement-induced structure produced, consumed, and transformed by protocol execution. Q2NSViz is built around a decoupled JSON/NDJSON trace contract, a Qt-free replay engine, and an interactive PyQt6 interface, making it a standalone companion to Q2NS and reusable by other simulation backends that emit the same trace format. By turning execution traces into navigable and reproducible visual artifacts, Q2NSViz provides a zero-coding tool for researchers and educators, narrowing the gap between abstract protocol logic and concrete execution.

AI.tldr: Q2NSViz is an open-source Python visualization tool that replays and inspects quantum network simulation traces, reconstructing time evolution including topology, qubits, classical bits, measurements, and entanglement relationships to bridge abstract protocol logic and concrete execution.
AI.motivation: Quantum networks have unique and non-classical features that make their simulation and intuitive understanding inherently difficult, creating a need for tools that expose dynamic entanglement-induced structure produced by protocol execution.
AI.method: Built around a decoupled JSON/NDJSON trace contract, a Qt-free replay engine, and an interactive PyQt6 interface; works as a standalone companion to Q2NS and reusable by other simulation backends emitting the same trace format.
AI.result: Provides a zero-coding tool that turns execution traces into navigable and reproducible visual artifacts, exposing physical connectivity and dynamic entanglement-induced structure.
AI.conclusion: Narrows the gap between abstract protocol logic and concrete execution, offering a useful tool for both researchers and educators.

title: Strain-Induced Detuning of a Dressed Nitrogen-Vacancy Qubit: Effective Two-Level Theory and Its Validity
summary: The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond can be operated as a microwave-dressed qubit. In the ideal two-level limit, its transition frequency is first-order insensitive to static magnetic fields, providing robustness against magnetic detuning noise. In practical diamond devices, however, residual transverse crystal strain mixes the $\ket{m_{s}=\pm1}$ spin sublevels and modifies the dressed qubit. In this study, we derive an analytical effective two-level model of a strained dressed NV qubit by perturbatively eliminating the far-detuned spectator state from the full three-level dressed Hamiltonian. We obtain closed-form expressions for the dressed-state splitting, the spin-locking mixing angle, and the longitudinal magnetic-field coupling. We show that transverse strain shifts the dressed-state resonance and tilts the spin-locking axis. These two effects restore a finite DC-field response and thereby quantify the loss of magnetic robustness. We demonstrate these features in simulated pulsed electron spin resonance spectra that incorporate rate-equation-based optical readout. We further derive exact validity criteria from the eigenvalues and spectator weights of the full three-level Hamiltonian. For practical use, we reduce these criteria to two controlled guidelines: the spectator-like branch must remain above the nominal upper dressed state, and its branch-specific admixture must remain small. A validity diagram over the axial-field--transverse-strain plane summarizes these approximate conditions and provides practical guidelines for designing dressed-NV sensing experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper analytically models how residual transverse crystal strain affects a microwave-dressed NV qubit in diamond. By perturbatively eliminating a spectator state, the authors derive closed-form expressions showing that strain shifts the dressed-state resonance and tilts the spin-locking axis, restoring a finite DC magnetic field response and degrading magnetic noise robustness. They provide exact validity criteria and practical guidelines (validity diagram) for designing robust dressed-NV sensors.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify how residual transverse crystal strain degrades the magnetic-field insensitivity of microwave-dressed NV qubits, and to provide practical design guidelines for robust sensing.
AI.method: Perturbative elimination of the far-detuned spectator state from the full three-level dressed Hamiltonian to derive an effective two-level model, providing closed-form analytical expressions for dressed-state splitting, spin-locking mixing angle, and longitudinal magnetic-field coupling. Reduced exact eigenvalue conditions to two practical guidelines.
AI.result: Transverse strain shifts the dressed-state resonance and tilts the spin-locking axis, restoring finite DC-field response and compromising magnetic robustness. Validity criteria reduced to: (1) the spectator-like branch must stay above the nominal upper dressed state, and (2) its branch-specific admixture must remain small. A validity diagram over axial-field–transverse-strain plane is provided.
AI.conclusion: The analytical model accurately captures strain-induced degradation of magnetic robustness in dressed NV qubits, and the derived validity diagram offers practical guidelines for designing strain-tolerant dressed-NV sensing experiments.

title: Sparse anisotropic positive maps for qutrit entanglement: exact indecomposability and PPT geometry
summary: Positive but not completely positive maps provide one of the most direct ways to detect entanglement beyond the positive-partial-transpose (PPT) criterion. We introduce and analyze an exactly solvable two-parameter family of sparse bistochastic positive maps on qutrits, in which two coherence channels are independently tuned by parameters $w$ and $z$. The sparse structure makes the full phase diagram analytic: positivity holds exactly on the square $0\le w,z\le2/3$, complete positivity on the smaller square $0\le w,z\le1/3$, and decomposability is lost precisely outside a quarter circle in the corner $w,z\ge1/3$. The indecomposable region is certified by explicit PPT entangled state adapted to the same witness geometry. At the endpoint $W_*=W(2/3,2/3)$ we construct a four-parameter family of PPT edge states of rank type $(5,5)$, derive their analytic detection region, and show that the corresponding rays are exposed faces of the PPT cone. Finally, although $W_*$ is not optimal, we give an explicit optimal refinement whose detection region on this family is strictly larger. The result is an analytically tractable qutrit setting in which positivity, indecomposability, PPT entanglement, optimality, and exposed convex geometry can be studied in a single framework.

AI.tldr: A two-parameter family of sparse bistochastic positive maps on qutrits is introduced, with analytic phase diagrams for positivity, complete positivity, and decomposability. PPT entangled edge states and exposed faces of the PPT cone are constructed, and optimal refinement is demonstrated.
AI.motivation: To provide an analytically tractable framework for studying positive maps, indecomposability, PPT entanglement, optimality, and exposed convex geometry in qutrit systems, extending entanglement detection beyond the PPT criterion.
AI.method: Introduce sparse bistochastic maps $W(w,z)$ on qutrits with two independently tuned coherence channels. Derive analytic conditions for positivity (square $0\le w,z\le2/3$), complete positivity (smaller square $0\le w,z\le1/3$), and decomposability (lost outside a quarter circle in $w,z\ge1/3$). Construct explicit PPT entangled states and a four-parameter family of PPT edge states of rank type $(5,5)$ at $W_*=W(2/3,2/3)$, with analytic detection region and exposed faces. Provide optimal refinement with strictly larger detection region.
AI.result: Full analytic phase diagram obtained: positivity on $[0,2/3]^2$, complete positivity on $[0,1/3]^2$, indecomposability beyond a quarter circle in $[1/3,\infty)^2$. PPT edge states of rank type $(5,5)$ constructed with analytic detection regions; corresponding rays are exposed faces of the PPT cone. An optimal refinement strictly improves detection on this family.
AI.conclusion: The constructed map family provides a complete, analytically solvable qutrit setting unifying positivity, indecomposability, PPT entanglement, optimality, and exposed convex geometry, enabling systematic study of entanglement detection beyond the PPT criterion.

title: Benchmarking loss functions for trainable quantum feature maps
summary: Many quantum machine learning models employ quantum feature maps to encode classical data into quantum states. While fixed feature maps often lack sufficient expressivity for complex nonlinear classification tasks, trainable quantum feature maps (TQFMs) enable adaptive quantum kernels with enhanced learning capability. Different loss functions can induce distinct optimization dynamics, yet their effects remain poorly understood. In this work, we apply the Log-Likelihood Loss function for TQFMs and provide a systematic comparison with Distance Loss and Measurement Loss. Through extensive numerical experiments, we compare their optimization dynamics, computational costs, and classification performance. Our results show that Log-Likelihood Loss consistently achieves more stable optimization than Measurement Loss while retaining linear computational complexity. The resulting benchmark offers practical guidance for balancing trainability, computational efficiency, and predictive performance in quantum kernel optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates Log-Likelihood Loss for trainable quantum feature maps, comparing it with Distance Loss and Measurement Loss, finding that Log-Likelihood Loss achieves more stable optimization with linear computational complexity.
AI.motivation: Trainable quantum feature maps enable adaptive quantum kernels but the effects of different loss functions on optimization dynamics remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Applied Log-Likelihood Loss to TQFMs and conducted systematic numerical experiments comparing optimization dynamics, computational costs, and classification performance against Distance Loss and Measurement Loss.
AI.result: Log-Likelihood Loss achieves more stable optimization than Measurement Loss while maintaining linear computational complexity.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides practical guidance for balancing trainability, computational efficiency, and predictive performance in quantum kernel optimization.

title: The Infinitesimal Structure of Quantum Information
summary: This paper establishes a rigorous, unified geometric framework for quantum state spaces by constructing smooth, regular embeddings into higher-order dual number algebras $\mathcal{Q}_N \equiv \mathbb{R}[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^{N^2-1})$, wherein every quantum state is faithfully represented as a non-reduced scheme-theoretic point. We show that under this unified family of truncated rings, the non-linear matrix commutators governing the Liouville-von Neumann dynamics map globally onto flat, linear, and rigid algebraic flows, establishing nilpotent dual algebras as a pristine geometric landscape for higher-dimensional quantum kinematics.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a geometric framework using dual number algebras to represent quantum states as non-reduced scheme points, transforming nonlinear quantum dynamics into linear algebraic flows.
AI.motivation: To establish a unified geometric framework for quantum state spaces that simplifies the nonlinear dynamics of quantum systems into linear, tractable algebraic structures.
AI.method: The authors construct smooth embeddings of quantum state spaces into higher-order dual number algebras $\mathcal{Q}_N \equiv \mathbb{R}[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^{N^2-1})$, representing quantum states as non-reduced scheme-theoretic points and analyzing the resulting algebraic flows.
AI.result: The nonlinear matrix commutators governing Liouville-von Neumann dynamics map globally onto flat, linear, and rigid algebraic flows within the nilpotent dual algebra framework.
AI.conclusion: Nilpotent dual algebras provide a pristine geometric landscape for studying higher-dimensional quantum kinematics, offering a linearized representation of quantum dynamics.

title: The Quantum Polariton Hamiltonian that Reproduces the Same High-Harmonic Generation Spectra as the Classical Hamiltonian in Strong Laser Fields
summary: This manuscript investigates the possibility of defining a quantum Hamiltonian that leads to the same high-harmonic generation (HHG) spectra as those predicted by Floquet theory in the regime where the number of infrared (IR) pump photons is much larger than the number of emitted UV photons. The key assumption underlying our derivation is that the intensity of the emitted high harmonics is many orders of magnitude smaller than that of the IR laser, and that the emission of the Nnt harmonic results from the absorption of N IR photons.

AI.tldr: This paper explores defining a quantum Hamiltonian that reproduces the HHG spectra from Floquet theory when IR pump photons far outnumber emitted UV photons, assuming emitted harmonics are much weaker than the IR laser and each harmonic results from absorbing N IR photons.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether a quantum Hamiltonian can be defined that yields the same high-harmonic generation spectra as Floquet theory, specifically in the regime where the number of IR pump photons greatly exceeds emitted UV photons.
AI.method: The authors derive a quantum Hamiltonian approach based on two key assumptions: (1) emitted high-harmonic intensity is orders of magnitude weaker than the IR laser, and (2) each Nth harmonic results from absorption of N IR photons.
AI.result: A quantum Hamiltonian formulation that matches Floquet theory predictions for HHG spectra under specified conditions.
AI.conclusion: It is possible to define a quantum Hamiltonian that reproduces Floquet-theory-predicted HHG spectra when the number of IR pump photons is much larger than emitted UV photons.

title: Fast measurement-based generation of large-scale Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state with atomic nuclear-spin qubits
summary: Large-scale Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger~(GHZ) state is useful for quantum technologies but difficult to be prepared. Here, we propose fast measurement-based preparation of large-scale GHZ states by a four-qubit quantum phase gate with nuclear-spin qubits of alkaline-earth-like atoms, which is named as quantum ferromagnetic gate~(QFG) due to its analogy to the alignment of molecular magnetic moments in a classical magnet. A high-fidelity Rydberg-mediated QFG can be realized in a time of $6π/Ω_{\text{m}}$ with $Ω_{\text{m}}$ the maximal Rydberg Rabi frequency. From a product state of three data atom and one ancilla atom, a gluing circuit with one QFG, two single-qubit gates, and a projective measurement of the ancilla can generate a 3-qubit GHZ state, and repetition of this gluing circuit can lead to 9, 27, 81, 243, $\cdots$-qubit GHZ states. Analyses based on currently available techniques show that a 243-qubit GHZ state is realizable, and more qubits can be entangled with higher detection fidelity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a fast, measurement-based method for preparing large-scale GHZ states using a four-qubit quantum phase gate (QFG) with nuclear-spin qubits of alkaline-earth-like atoms. A gluing circuit can generate 3-qubit GHZ states and be repeated to scale to 9, 27, 81, 243-qubit states, with analysis suggesting 243-qubit GHZ states are feasible with current technology.
AI.motivation: Large-scale GHZ states are useful for quantum technologies but difficult to prepare, motivating the search for a more efficient and scalable generation method.
AI.method: The method uses a Rydberg-mediated four-qubit quantum ferromagnetic gate (QFG) with nuclear-spin qubits of alkaline-earth-like atoms. A gluing circuit (one QFG, two single-qubit gates, and a projective measurement of the ancilla) generates a 3-qubit GHZ state from a product state. This circuit is repeated iteratively to scale to larger GHZ states (9, 27, 81, 243, ... qubits).
AI.result: A high-fidelity Rydberg-mediated QFG can be realized in time $6\pi/\Omega_{\text{m}}$. Analysis based on current techniques shows a 243-qubit GHZ state is realizable, and more qubits can be entangled with higher detection fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed measurement-based approach enables fast, scalable generation of large-scale GHZ states, with 243-qubit states achievable using current technology.

title: Forked Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Non-Markovian Open Quantum Dynamics and Control
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a pathway to reunify the simulation and control of quantum systems, in which these two tasks are typically decoupled in traditional strategies. However, most work remains confined to Markovian environments. When applied to non-Markovian systems, standard PINN architectures fail to converge reliably due to multi-objective optimization conflicts arising from the coupled differential equations. To address this fundamental limitation, we extend our previously proposed forked PINN (FPINN) by incorporating a dedicated control branch. By decoupling the optimization objectives at the gradient level via selective gradient flow, our method turns a previously intractable multi-task optimization into a well-conditioned one, allowing simulation and control to be optimized jointly without compromise. Numerical simulations on a two-qubit Heisenberg XXX model confirm that our framework faithfully reproduces the features of non-Markovian dynamics, including decoherence and information backflow. Taking a state-preparation task on the same model as an example, our FPINN achieves higher fidelity than gradient ascent pulse engineering, chopped random basis, and standard PINNs, with the advantage becoming more pronounced as the environment becomes more dissipative and more Markovian. The generated pulses are also noticeably smoother, which is advantageous for experimental implementation. Our framework thus provides a unified, end-to-end differentiable paradigm for simulation and control of open quantum systems, with potential implications for quantum computing, simulation, and control.

AI.tldr: This paper extends forked PINNs (FPINNs) with a control branch to jointly simulate and control non-Markovian open quantum systems. By decoupling optimization objectives via selective gradient flow, it resolves convergence failures of standard PINNs. On a two-qubit Heisenberg XXX model, FPINN achieves higher state-preparation fidelity than GRAPE, CRAB, and standard PINNs, especially under dissipative/Markovian conditions, and produces smoother control pulses.
AI.motivation: Standard PINNs fail to converge for non-Markovian quantum systems due to multi-objective optimization conflicts from coupled differential equations. Current work on PINNs for quantum control remains mostly confined to Markovian environments, leaving a gap for non-Markovian scenarios where simulation and control are typically decoupled.
AI.method: The authors extend their previously proposed forked PINN (FPINN) by adding a dedicated control branch. They decouple optimization objectives at the gradient level using selective gradient flow, turning a multi-task optimization problem into a well-conditioned one, enabling joint optimization of simulation and control.
AI.result: On a two-qubit Heisenberg XXX model, the FPINN faithfully reproduces non-Markovian dynamics (decoherence, information backflow). For state-preparation tasks, FPINN achieves higher fidelity than GRAPE, CRAB, and standard PINNs, with advantages growing in more dissipative and more Markovian environments. Generated pulses are smoother, benefiting experimental implementation.
AI.conclusion: The FPINN framework provides a unified, end-to-end differentiable paradigm for simulation and control of open quantum systems, with potential implications for quantum computing, simulation, and control.

title: Activating thermally charged quantum batteries in finite time: Thermodynamic trade-offs between correlations, work, and information
summary: Thermally charged quantum batteries provide a stable and easy-to-have energy resource, but remain passive and therefore do not allow useful energy extraction on demand via unitary operations. We introduce a time-dependent stirring protocol that activates a thermally charged quantum battery through a time-dependent coupling to an auxiliary activator, thereby generating correlations that drive the battery into an active state. Accounting explicitly for the energetic cost of the stirring process, the entropic cost of correlation generation and the activation time, we derive bounds on the maximal net extractable energy. Incorporating projective measurement on the activator and exploiting the information gained through the measurement further enhances the extractable energy. As an experimentally relevant example, we analyze a waveguide-QED setup where a harmonic-oscillator battery (waveguide) is stirred and monitored by a two-level system. We characterize the performance of the protocol in terms of net extractable energy (net ergotropy) and power output.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a time-dependent stirring protocol to activate thermally charged quantum batteries, enabling on-demand energy extraction via correlation generation with an auxiliary activator. It derives bounds on net extractable energy considering costs, shows that measurement on the activator enhances performance, and analyzes a waveguide-QED implementation.
AI.motivation: Thermally charged quantum batteries are passive (cannot perform unitary work extraction on demand). The authors aim to activate them through a controlled stirring process that generates correlations, enabling useful energy extraction.
AI.method: The protocol uses time-dependent coupling between a passive thermal quantum battery and an auxiliary activator to generate correlations. It accounts for energetic costs of stirring, entropic costs of correlation generation, and activation time. Additionally, projective measurement on the activator is incorporated to improve extractable energy. The scheme is analyzed in a waveguide-QED setup with a harmonic-oscillator battery coupled to a two-level system.
AI.result: Bounds on maximal net extractable energy (net ergotropy) are derived. The protocol successfully activates the battery, and incorporating measurement on the activator further enhances extractable energy and power output.
AI.conclusion: Thermally charged quantum batteries can be activated by a stirring protocol with an auxiliary activator, generating correlations that enable on-demand work extraction. The approach is experimentally feasible in waveguide-QED systems, with measurement-enhanced performance.

title: Entropy Transport in Programmable Quantum Junctions
summary: We show that driven qubit junctions enable programmable control of physical entropy transport, with entropy conductance governed by quantum dynamics rather than by reservoir parameters alone. By comparing two simple quantum architectures -- a driven single-qubit junction and a driven two-qubit junction -- we find that the two-qubit junction enhances entropy transfer while requiring substantially lower driving power than its single-qubit counterpart. We further reveal two non-intuitive effects in both junctions: a sizable coherent contribution to the entropy current that emerges only under resonant driving, and negative differential entropy conductance, where increasing the thermal bias suppresses entropy flow into the probe reservoir. These results identify quantum logic architectures as programmable devices for entropy transport and suggest routes toward quantum feedback control, reservoir protection and refrigeration in driven quantum circuits.

AI.tldr: Driven qubit junctions enable programmable entropy transport, with two-qubit designs offering higher efficiency than single-qubit ones. Key findings include coherent entropy current under resonant driving and negative differential entropy conductance.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that quantum logic architectures can serve as programmable devices for controlling entropy transport, beyond traditional reservoir-parameter-based approaches.
AI.method: Comparison of two quantum architectures: a driven single-qubit junction and a driven two-qubit junction, analyzing entropy conductance under various driving conditions.
AI.result: Two-qubit junction enhances entropy transfer with lower driving power; coherent entropy current emerges under resonant driving; negative differential entropy conductance is observed where increasing thermal bias suppresses entropy flow.
AI.conclusion: Driven qubit junctions are viable programmable entropy transport devices, with implications for quantum feedback control, reservoir protection, and refrigeration.

title: Quantum tests via inequalities for joint statistics
summary: In this work we derive statistical inequalities whose violation is equivalent to the impossibility of describing the data by a genuine joint probability distribution. So they are witnesses of the failure of a common probability space. We examine whether the most significant quantum quasidistributions violate these inequalities. We examine also whether these inequalitites are violated by the joint distributions derived form a noisy joint measurement. As a relevant example we find violations for the maximally mixed state, as well as cases where all system states violate them. This points to the idea that these results are more than a property of the system states, but are instead a property of the statistical structure of quantum mechanics.

AI.tldr: The paper derives statistical inequalities that, when violated, indicate the impossibility of describing data with a genuine joint probability distribution, serving as witnesses for the failure of a common probability space. The authors examine violations by quantum quasidistributions and noisy joint measurements, finding that even the maximally mixed state and all system states can violate them, suggesting these violations reflect the statistical structure of quantum mechanics rather than just specific states.
AI.motivation: To derive statistical inequalities that serve as witnesses for the failure of a common probability space in describing quantum data, and to explore whether such violations are intrinsic to quantum mechanics rather than state-dependent.
AI.method: Derivation of statistical inequalities whose violation indicates the impossibility of a genuine joint probability distribution; testing these inequalities against quantum quasidistributions and noisy joint measurement distributions.
AI.result: Violations are found for the maximally mixed state and cases where all system states violate the inequalities, indicating the effect is not state-specific.
AI.conclusion: The observed violations are more than a property of particular quantum states; they reflect a fundamental property of the statistical structure of quantum mechanics itself.

title: Constructing mode-resolved quantum optical models for emitters in photonic crystals
summary: Recent advances are enabling quantum emitters to interact with photonic crystals, whose electromagnetic modes exhibit complex dispersion relations, spatial mode structure, and polarization textures. However, modeling light-matter behavior in these systems faces a persistent trade-off: electromagnetic approaches based on Maxwell-equation solvers provide realistic vectorial descriptions but are difficult to integrate with quantum many-body and non-perturbative methods, whereas simplified quantum-optical lattice models are tractable but typically rely on scalar and spatially independent light-matter couplings that miss essential features of these structured photonic environments. Here, we introduce a constructive framework to derive quantum-optical lattice descriptions that overcome this trade-off. Combining symmetry-constrained tight-binding constructions with numerically computed photonic band structures and field profiles, our method yields minimal, symmetry-enforced lattice Hamiltonians that reproduce the target photonic dispersion while retaining the mode-resolved (position- and polarization-dependent) structure of the light-matter coupling. We show that these models recover Green's-function-based emitter dynamics in the perturbative regime, while providing access to non-perturbative quantum dynamical simulations beyond emitter-only descriptions. As a proof of principle, we apply the framework to a two-dimensional photonic crystal and show that it captures polarization-dependent directional emission inaccessible to scalar models, while enabling the analysis of non-Markovian light-matter dynamics and entanglement. Our results provide a practical bridge between classical electromagnetic simulation tools and quantum-optical many-body and non-Markovian modeling in photonic crystal settings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a constructive framework that bridges classical electromagnetic simulations and quantum-optical many-body models for photonic crystal systems. By combining symmetry-constrained tight-binding constructions with numerically computed photonic band structures and field profiles, the method yields minimal lattice Hamiltonians that accurately reproduce both photonic dispersion and vectorial light-matter coupling (position- and polarization-dependent), enabling non-perturbative quantum dynamics beyond emitter-only descriptions.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches face a trade-off: Maxwell-equation solvers provide realistic vectorial descriptions but are hard to integrate with quantum many-body/non-perturbative methods, while simplified quantum-optical lattice models are tractable but miss essential features of structured photonic environments due to scalar, spatially independent light-matter couplings.
AI.method: The framework combines symmetry-constrained tight-binding constructions with numerically computed photonic band structures and field profiles to derive minimal, symmetry-enforced lattice Hamiltonians that reproduce the target photonic dispersion while retaining mode-resolved (position- and polarization-dependent) light-matter coupling structure.
AI.result: The models recover Green's-function-based emitter dynamics in the perturbative regime and enable non-perturbative quantum dynamical simulations beyond emitter-only descriptions. Applied to a 2D photonic crystal, the framework captures polarization-dependent directional emission inaccessible to scalar models and enables analysis of non-Markovian dynamics and entanglement.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a practical bridge between classical electromagnetic simulation tools and quantum-optical many-body and non-Markovian modeling in photonic crystal settings, overcoming the previous trade-off between realism and tractability.

title: James-Stein estimation for quantum sensing schemes
summary: Quantum metrology protocols typically consist of four steps: state preparation, evolution, measurement, and data processing. Often, the first three steps are prioritised when designing a scheme as they contain all the quantum elements. The data analysis is generally considered an add-on with an implicit assumption that this step is well behaved and so standard data techniques can be applied. However, the situation can be more nuanced, such as when the available data are limited. In limited-data quantum metrology the choice of data analysis technique and cost function of the estimator is of great importance, and a reliable prior distribution of the unknown parameters is required for Bayesian analysis. An interesting question is what we should do when no such prior is available. In this work, we consider how the James-Stein estimator can give significant advantages when measuring multiple unknown parameters with limited data and, importantly, does not require any prior distribution. We demonstrate the advantage by applying this methodology to simple quantum metrology schemes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using the James-Stein estimator for limited-data quantum metrology, demonstrating advantages when measuring multiple unknown parameters without requiring a prior distribution.
AI.motivation: Data analysis in quantum metrology is often treated as an add-on, but with limited data the choice of technique matters significantly. Bayesian methods require a prior distribution, which may not always be available.
AI.method: The authors apply the James-Stein estimator to simple quantum metrology schemes, comparing its performance against standard estimators in the limited-data regime without requiring prior distributions.
AI.result: The James-Stein estimator provides significant advantages over conventional approaches when measuring multiple unknown parameters with limited data, without needing any prior distribution.
AI.conclusion: The James-Stein estimator is a powerful tool for limited-data quantum metrology, filling an important gap when prior information is unavailable and standard data techniques are inadequate.

title: Quantum metrology with undetected mid-infrared photons for applied non-destructive testing
summary: Metrology with undetected photons is an emerging technique that leverages quantum effects and photon correlations (entanglement) to retrieve valuable information in a target spectral range (e.g., mid-infrared, mid-IR) using measurements in an easily accessible domain (e.g., visible, near-IR). The underlying quantum process of spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) is utilized to generate non-degenerate correlated signal and idler photons to serve as detection and probing photons, respectively. Sensing with undetected photons enables important advantages, such as ultra-low probe powers, room-temperature operation, and shot-noise-limited detection. In this contribution, we apply a quantum nonlinear interferometer based on an SPDC source to perform applied mid-IR spectroscopy, mid-IR microscopy, and mid-IR optical coherence tomography (OCT) as among the most promising techniques for quantum-based routine non-destructive testing. Moreover, we characterize the system, benchmark it against classical systems, and provide a prospective outlook for this new technology.

AI.tldr: This paper applies quantum nonlinear interferometry using SPDC for mid-IR spectroscopy, microscopy, and OCT with undetected photons, offering ultra-low probe power, room-temperature operation, and shot-noise-limited detection, while benchmarking against classical systems.
AI.motivation: To leverage quantum effects (photon correlations/entanglement) for retrieving information in the mid-IR range using visible/near-IR measurements, enabling non-destructive testing with low probe power and room-temperature operation.
AI.method: A quantum nonlinear interferometer based on a spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) source generating non-degenerate correlated signal and idler photons; signal photons are detected in the visible/near-IR while idler photons probe the sample in the mid-IR.
AI.result: Demonstrated mid-IR spectroscopy, microscopy, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) with undetected photons; system characterized and benchmarked against classical counterparts.
AI.conclusion: Metrology with undetected photons via SPDC-based quantum nonlinear interferometry is a promising technology for routine non-destructive testing, offering key advantages over classical mid-IR techniques.

title: Entanglement and Optical Nonreciprocity in spontaneous Raman Scattering
summary: Inelastic light scattering is a central tool for sample characterization and label-free imaging across the physical and life sciences. Recent work has suggested that scattered light can also exhibit nonclassical correlations. Here, we develop a microscopic theory of Raman scattering that connects naturally to established descriptions of entangled-photon generation in three- and four-wave mixing, while capturing essential differences arising from the resonant, dissipative character of Raman scattering. Using a cumulant-expansion approach, we analyze the entanglement structure of the scattered sidebands and identify signatures that distinguish Raman-mediated correlations from those generated in conventional off-resonant nonlinear wave mixing. In particular, we show that Raman scattering induces chiral couplings between Stokes and anti-Stokes sidebands, leading to nonreciprocal amplification of coherent seed fields. These results establish a theoretical framework for Raman-based quantum photonic protocols and suggest routes toward quantum-enhanced Raman spectroscopy and imaging.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a microscopic theory of Raman scattering that bridges it with entangled-photon generation in nonlinear wave mixing, revealing chiral couplings between Stokes and anti-Stokes sidebands that lead to nonreciprocal amplification and establishing a framework for quantum-enhanced Raman spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: Recent work suggested scattered light can exhibit nonclassical correlations, but a rigorous theoretical connection between Raman scattering and established descriptions of entangled-photon generation was lacking, particularly regarding the resonant, dissipative nature of Raman processes.
AI.method: The authors develop a microscopic theory of Raman scattering using a cumulant-expansion approach to analyze entanglement structure and compare it with conventional three- and four-wave mixing descriptions.
AI.result: Raman scattering induces chiral couplings between Stokes and anti-Stokes sidebands, leading to nonreciprocal amplification of coherent seed fields, with entanglement signatures that distinguish Raman-mediated correlations from those in off-resonant nonlinear wave mixing.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a theoretical framework for Raman-based quantum photonic protocols and suggest routes toward quantum-enhanced Raman spectroscopy and imaging.

title: Quantum PDE Solvers in Practice: Application-Driven Benchmarking of the Heat Equation
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE26, IEEE Quantum Week 2026); to appear in the conference proceedings
summary: Quantum PDE solvers are difficult to evaluate in practice because published studies use different discretizations, output models, reconstruction rules, and hardware assumptions. We present a reproducible, application-driven benchmark for the 1-D Dirichlet heat equation that compares eleven kernels under the same problem instances and readout contract. The benchmark covers coherent linear solvers (HHL, QSVT, and QLS-Fourier), VQLS, imaginary-time methods (QITE, var-QITE, and AVQDS), real-time Hamiltonian simulation and unitary dilations (Hamiltonian simulation, Schade-Hamiltonian, and Schr"odingerisation), and the spectral quantum simulation method (QSM). We use three initial conditions, four grid sizes from $n=4$ to $7$ qubits ($N=16$ to $128$), a CFL-like ratio $r\approx0.4$, and final time $T=1$. Statevector, ideal-shot ($10^5$ shots per step), and noisy Aer backends separate algorithmic, sampling, and device-noise errors. On statevector, QSM and Schade-Hamiltonian reproduce the semi-discrete reference to floating-point precision, Schr"odingerisation reaches approximately $10^{-4}$ error, and QITE is the strongest non-transform method for smooth data. Under the fixed-shot setting, HHL degrades to approximately $0.79$ relative $\ell_2$ error, while several low-depth or postselected methods become readout-limited. A norm-mismatch ablation attributes 23--29% of the $n=7$ smooth-initial-condition error of Hamiltonian simulation, AVQDS, and QLS-Fourier to reconstruction normalization. Compact observables, including total thermal energy and individual Fourier-mode weights, require 1--3 orders of magnitude fewer shots than full-field reconstruction. The resulting public benchmark provides a practical guide for selecting quantum PDE solvers.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a reproducible benchmark comparing 11 quantum PDE solvers for the 1-D heat equation under consistent problem instances, discretizations, and readout conditions, using statevector, shot-based, and noisy backends to separate algorithmic, sampling, and device errors.
AI.motivation: Quantum PDE solvers are difficult to evaluate fairly because prior studies use inconsistent discretizations, output models, reconstruction rules, and hardware assumptions, making cross-method comparison unreliable.
AI.method: Eleven quantum kernels were tested on the 1-D Dirichlet heat equation with three initial conditions, four grid sizes (n=4–7 qubits), CFL ratio r≈0.4, and final time T=1. Methods include HHL, QSVT, QLS-Fourier, VQLS, QITE, var-QITE, AVQDS, Hamiltonian simulation, Schade-Hamiltonian, Schrödingerisation, and QSM. Benchmarks used statevector, ideal-shot (10⁵ shots/step), and noisy Aer backends.
AI.result: QSM and Schade-Hamiltonian achieve floating-point precision on statevector; Schrödingerisation reaches ~10⁻⁴ error; QITE is best among non-transform methods for smooth data. Under fixed shots, HHL degrades to ~0.79 relative ℓ₂ error. Norm-mismatch ablation attributes 23–29% of error for n=7 smooth IC to reconstruction normalization. Compact observables need 1–3 orders of magnitude fewer shots than full-field reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides a practical guide for selecting quantum PDE solvers, highlighting trade-offs between accuracy, shot efficiency, and noise resilience across methods.

title: Thermally Activated Long-Range Entanglement from Non-Abelian Conservation Laws
summary: Thermal noise ordinarily suppresses quantum entanglement. We show that a strong non-Abelian conservation law can convert local thermal fluctuations into an unbounded operational resource. For a broad class of finite-range $SU(2)$-invariant spin chains restricted to the global-singlet sector, an explicit representation-space protocol yields $Y_N=\frac12\log_2 N+O_β(1)$, and hence $E_{\mathrm{D}}\geq Y_N$, throughout a finite high-temperature interval. Local thermal fluctuations produce subsystem spins $j\sim\sqrt N$, whose globally locked irreducible representations contain $\log_2(2j+1)\sim\frac12\log_2N$ ebits. An exactly solvable dimer chain exhibits a sharper effect: its zero-temperature state is unentangled across the cut, whereas every fixed $T>0$ produces $E_{\mathrm{D}}=\frac{1}{2}\log_2 N+C(T)+o(1)$, with crossover scale $T_*(N)\simΔ/\ln N$. Exact diagonalization of a nonintegrable chain is consistent with the predicted scaling. Thus heating can activate system-size-diverging distillable entanglement across a macroscopic bipartition when thermalization is confined by a non-Abelian conservation law.

AI.tldr: Non-Abelian conservation laws (specifically SU(2) symmetry) can convert local thermal fluctuations into unbounded distillable entanglement that scales as ~½log₂N across a bipartition, even at finite high temperatures, contrary to the usual expectation that thermal noise suppresses entanglement.
AI.motivation: To challenge the conventional wisdom that thermal noise always suppresses quantum entanglement by showing that a strong non-Abelian conservation law can transform thermal fluctuations into an operational resource for entanglement.
AI.method: The authors analyze SU(2)-invariant spin chains in the global-singlet sector using representation theory, derive an expression Y_N = ½log₂N + O_β(1) for distillable entanglement, study an exactly solvable dimer chain, and perform exact diagonalization of a nonintegrable chain to confirm predicted scaling.
AI.result: Distillable entanglement E_D ≥ ½log₂N at finite high temperatures; dimer chain yields E_D = ½log₂N + C(T) + o(1) for any T>0 while zero-temperature state is unentangled; exact diagonalization of nonintegrable chain consistent with predicted scaling.
AI.conclusion: Heating can activate system-size-diverging distillable entanglement across a macroscopic bipartition when thermalization is confined by a non-Abelian conservation law.

title: When Close Enough Is Not Enough: Autoregressive Drift in Quantum Circuit Synthesis
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables, IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE) 2026
summary:
Quantum circuit optimization for fault-tolerant computing requires exact functional equivalence while minimizing expensive non-Clifford resources such as T gates. We study this problem using a compact 44.8M-parameter encoder-decoder transformer with structured circuit tokenization, evaluating on parameterized circuits (2-6 qubits) and Clifford+T circuits (3-6 qubits). On parameterized circuits, a hybrid approach -- structure from the transformer, angles from classical optimization -- achieves median fidelity 1.000 on 3-6 qubit circuits. On Clifford+T circuits, where all gates are discrete and no post-processing is possible, the model learns valid syntax and accurate T-Count statistics, yet exact equivalence degrades sharply with target length -- from 88% on circuits with <=9 gates to near zero beyond 26 gates.
  We trace this failure to autoregressive drift: early-token divergence cascading irrecoverably through left-to-right decoding. Two levers partially mitigate the drift: inference-time strategies that generate multiple candidates and select via equivalence verification raise exact-match rates from 7% to 22.5%, while scaling training data by 2.5x pushes them to 39.5%. Yet the degradation with target length persists -- even with more data, exact equivalence drops from 94% on short circuits to under 4% beyond 26 gates.
  The contrast between settings is our central finding: when approximate outputs can be rescued by post-processing, the transformer succeeds; when exact discrete correctness is required, autoregressive drift limits reliability, with both inference-time search and data scaling as effective levers while training-side fine-tuning and model-level diversification are not.

AI.tldr: A transformer-based approach for quantum circuit optimization achieves high fidelity in parameterized circuits via hybrid post-processing, but fails on exact discrete Clifford+T optimization due to autoregressive drift, where inference-time search and data scaling partially mitigate but cannot fully overcome length-dependent degradation.
AI.motivation: To study the feasibility of transformer-based quantum circuit optimization for fault-tolerant computing, which requires exact functional equivalence while minimizing non-Clifford resources (T gates), and to understand the limitations of autoregressive models in discrete exact settings versus approximate settings with post-processing.
AI.method: A compact 44.8M-parameter encoder-decoder transformer with structured circuit tokenization, evaluated on parameterized circuits (2-6 qubits) and Clifford+T circuits (3-6 qubits). For parameterized circuits, a hybrid approach uses transformer structure with classical angle optimization. For Clifford+T circuits, autoregressive decoding is used directly. Inference-time search (multiple candidates with equivalence verification) and data scaling (2.5x) are tested as mitigation strategies.
AI.result: On parameterized circuits, median fidelity 1.000 on 3-6 qubits. On Clifford+T circuits, exact equivalence drops from 88% (<=9 gates) to near zero (>26 gates). Inference-time search raises exact-match from 7% to 22.5%; data scaling (2.5x) pushes to 39.5%. Even with more data, exact equivalence drops from 94% (short) to <4% (>26 gates). Training-side fine-tuning and model-level diversification are ineffective.
AI.conclusion: Transformers succeed for quantum circuit optimization when approximate outputs can be rescued by post-processing, but fail for exact discrete correctness due to autoregressive drift. Inference-time search and data scaling are effective levers, while training-side fine-tuning and model diversification are not. The degradation with target length persists regardless of data scaling.

title: A Variational Surrogate Approach to Finite-Horizon Quantum Control via Hardware-Efficient Ansatz
summary: We present a variational quantum framework for finite-horizon quantum control based on hardware-efficient ansätze. The objective is to steer a quantum system from a given initial state to a desired target state over a fixed time horizon by minimizing a terminal cost defined in terms of state fidelity. Instead of explicitly synthesizing time-dependent control fields or enforcing Hamiltonian reachability constraints, the proposed method reformulates the control objective as a variational optimization problem in which a hardware-efficient parameterized quantum circuit provides a surrogate parameterization of the terminal evolution. The circuit consists of alternating layers of single-qubit rotations and entangling gates, whose parameters are optimized using classical routines to minimize the terminal infidelity. This formulation avoids reliance on problem-specific or physics-inspired ansätze, providing a flexible and implementation-friendly approach compatible with near-term quantum devices. Numerical experiments on multi-qubit state-transfer benchmarks demonstrate high-fidelity state transfer while highlighting the trade-off between ansatz expressivity, optimization complexity, and scalability with respect to system size and circuit depth.

AI.tldr: A variational quantum framework for finite-horizon quantum control that uses hardware-efficient ansätze to steer quantum systems from initial to target states, reformulating the control problem as a variational optimization of parameterized quantum circuits to minimize terminal infidelity.
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum control approach that avoids explicit time-dependent field synthesis and problem-specific ansätze, making it flexible and compatible with near-term quantum devices.
AI.method: The method reformulates quantum control as a variational optimization problem using hardware-efficient parameterized quantum circuits (alternating layers of single-qubit rotations and entangling gates) as surrogate parameterizations of terminal evolution. Parameters are optimized via classical routines to minimize terminal infidelity (based on state fidelity).
AI.result: Numerical experiments on multi-qubit state-transfer benchmarks demonstrate high-fidelity state transfer, and reveal trade-offs between ansatz expressivity, optimization complexity, and scalability with system size and circuit depth.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a flexible, implementation-friendly approach to quantum control suitable for near-term quantum devices, with demonstrated high-fidelity results on multi-qubit benchmarks.

title: A Quantum Computing Approach to Track Reconstruction in Strip-Type Detectors
summary: This study investigates the use of quantum annealing for particle track reconstruction in strip-type gaseous detectors. In such detectors, ghost hits and multiple hit combinations can turn pattern recognition into a combinatorial optimization problem. We formulate two reconstruction subproblems as quadratic unconstrained binary optimization problems. The first subproblem selects detector hits associated with a single photon track inside a localized candidate region. The second subproblem selects cluster triplets from different detector layers so that multiple track candidates can be handled within a single quantum processing unit(QPU) submission. The proposed formulations are tested using simulated DAMSA detector events. For the single track hit selection task, the QPU based reconstruction gives position and angular resolutions close to those obtained with a Kalman based reconstruction. In the simultaneous association task, valid cluster triplets are first extracted from the QPU samples and then connected using an association rule based on graph connectivity to construct track candidates. The DAMSA event topology studied here has low pileup and is dominated by the two photon signal from axion-like particle(ALP) decay. In this setting, the results show that the QUBO formulations can reproduce local reconstruction decisions. This provides a practical basis for further studies of reconstruction methods that combine quantum and classical computing in more complex tracking environments.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using quantum annealing to solve combinatorial optimization problems in particle track reconstruction for strip-type gaseous detectors, demonstrating that QUBO formulations can match classical Kalman-based reconstruction performance in low-pileup DAMSA detector environments, particularly for axion-like particle decay signals.
AI.motivation: To address the combinatorial explosion of ghost hits and multiple hit combinations in strip-type gaseous detectors, which makes pattern recognition a challenging optimization problem that could benefit from quantum computing approaches.
AI.method: Two reconstruction subproblems are formulated as QUBO problems: (1) selecting detector hits associated with a single photon track in a localized candidate region, and (2) selecting cluster triplets from different detector layers to handle multiple track candidates in a single QPU submission. Simulated DAMSA detector events are used for testing.
AI.result: For single track hit selection, QPU-based reconstruction achieves position and angular resolutions close to Kalman-based reconstruction. For simultaneous association, valid cluster triplets are extracted from QPU samples and connected via graph connectivity-based association rules to construct track candidates.
AI.conclusion: QUBO formulations can reproduce local reconstruction decisions in low-pileup DAMSA event topology dominated by two-photon signals from ALP decay, providing a foundation for future hybrid quantum-classical reconstruction methods in more complex tracking environments.

title: The Resolution of the Identity as a Generator of Exact Integral Identities: A Coherent-State Approach
summary: The resolution of the identity is typically utilized as a passive representation tool in standard quantum mechanics textbooks. In this paper, we reinterpret this traditional perspective by introducing the resolution of the identity associated with Glauber coherent states as a direct generator of exact complex Gaussian integral identities. By systematically projecting the continuous coherent-state completeness relation onto the discrete Fock basis, highly generalized Gaussian integral relations emerge naturally as a direct consequence of state preservation, rather than being introduced as independent mathematical postulates. We demonstrate that this overarching formal structure simultaneously dictates both discrete (Kronecker delta) and continuous (Dirac delta) localization kernels under appropriate basis projections, providing a sharp conceptual contrast between the structural features of overcomplete and strictly orthogonal representations. Crucially, we highlight an intriguing non-commuting behavior in the parameter limits of the master identity. Requiring only the elementary properties of coherent states and the Dirac formalism, this approach offers a transparent and visually intuitive illustration of how Hilbert-space completeness inherently encodes vast libraries of exact, solvable mathematical relations -- providing a unifying perspective suitable for advanced undergraduate and graduate instruction.

AI.tldr: The resolution of identity from Glauber coherent states is reinterpreted as a generator of exact complex Gaussian integral identities, unifying discrete and continuous localization kernels through Hilbert-space completeness.
AI.motivation: To move beyond the passive textbook role of the resolution of identity and reveal it as an active generator of exact integral identities, providing a unified conceptual framework for understanding completeness in Hilbert space.
AI.method: Projecting the continuous coherent-state completeness relation onto the discrete Fock basis, deriving generalized Gaussian integral identities as a direct consequence of state preservation rather than independent postulates.
AI.result: The formalism simultaneously yields both Kronecker delta (discrete) and Dirac delta (continuous) localization kernels, exposing non-commuting parameter limits in the master identity and contrasting overcomplete versus orthogonal representations.
AI.conclusion: Hilbert-space completeness inherently encodes vast families of solvable mathematical relations, offering a transparent pedagogical approach suitable for advanced instruction that requires only elementary coherent-state properties and Dirac formalism.

title: Detecting Phishing in Ethereum Networks using Quantum Machine Learning
summary: This article explores the potential of Quantum Machine Learning (QML), specifically assessing a Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) and a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) for detecting anomalies in real-world financial transaction data. While these QML methods outperform statistical methods, they fall short of cutting-edge deep learning techniques. To bridge this gap, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical ensemble framework that leverages the strengths of both domains. We demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting phishing in Ethereum transaction networks by combining complementary algorithms. The QSVM, whether used individually or in an ensemble, consistently delivered the lowest false negatives and higher recall rates, that are crucial for anomaly detection. To enhance individual models, we encoded the data using novel cascaded Quantum Random Access Coding (QRAC) schemes and compared it with the popular encoding ZZ feature map on both simulators and the IBM Heron quantum processor. For both QSVM and VQC, we consistently observed improvements (13% for QRAC-VQC and 3% for QRAC-QSVM) of QRAC over the ZZ feature map. Notably, certain QML algorithms exhibit remarkable resilience on the IBM Heron quantum processor, approaching simulator-level performance on devices with high quantum volume. This observation underscores the promise of QML despite hardware limitations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical ensemble framework for financial anomaly detection, showing improved performance over individual quantum ML methods by using cascaded QRAC encoding schemes, with QML algorithms demonstrating resilience on IBM Heron quantum processors.
AI.motivation: To bridge the performance gap between quantum ML methods (QSVM, VQC) and cutting-edge deep learning techniques for detecting anomalies in financial transaction data, particularly phishing in Ethereum transaction networks.
AI.method: Proposes a hybrid quantum-classical ensemble framework combining QSVM and VQC with novel cascaded QRAC encoding schemes; compared against ZZ feature map on simulators and IBM Heron quantum processor.
AI.result: QRAC encoding improved performance by 13% for QRAC-VQC and 3% for QRAC-QSVM over ZZ feature map; QSVM delivered lowest false negatives and highest recall; QML algorithms showed remarkable resilience on IBM Heron, approaching simulator-level performance.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical ensemble framework effectively bridges the gap between QML and deep learning for anomaly detection; QRAC encoding consistently outperforms ZZ feature map; QML shows promise despite current hardware limitations.

title: End-to-End Quantum Key Distribution Across Hybrid Fiber and Free-Space Links with All-Optical Encoding Conversion
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) promises information-theoretically secure communication, but future networks must bridge fiber and free-space links that naturally employ different photonic encodings, namely time-bin in fiber and polarization in free space. Here we demonstrate a complete hybrid fiber and free-space QKD link that bridges both media within a single end-to-end protocol, converting between the two encodings entirely in the optical domain. Using the decoy-state BB84 protocol operating at 1550 nm, we demonstrate continuous secure-key generation over a 90 m outdoor free-space link. The system operates across atmospheric conditions spanning more than two orders of magnitude in the refractive-index structure parameter Cn^2, from strong daytime turbulence to quiescent nighttime conditions, and we further validate photon-level operation over a 750 m free-space extension. Throughout, the link maintains a session-mean quantum bit error rate (QBER) of 5.6-6.8%, well below the 11% BB84 security threshold. The encoding conversion is performed entirely in the optical domain without measurement or state reconstruction, preserving the security assumptions of the BB84 protocol. Consequently, the time-bin-to-polarization (T2P) and polarization-to-time-bin (P2T) converters remain part of the untrusted quantum channel rather than trusted intermediate nodes. These results establish secure photonic encoding conversion as a practical interface between fiber and free-space quantum communication platforms, providing a building block for future quantum networks applications.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a hybrid fiber and free-space QKD system that converts between time-bin (fiber) and polarization (free-space) encodings entirely in the optical domain, achieving continuous secure-key generation over a 90 m outdoor link with QBER of 5.6-6.8%, well below the 11% security threshold.
AI.motivation: Future quantum networks must bridge fiber and free-space links that inherently use different photonic encodings (time-bin vs. polarization), requiring a practical interface that maintains end-to-end security without trusted intermediate nodes.
AI.method: The system uses decoy-state BB84 protocol at 1550 nm with optical-domain encoding converters (time-bin-to-polarization T2P and polarization-to-time-bin P2T) that remain part of the untrusted quantum channel, tested over a 90 m outdoor free-space link across diverse atmospheric turbulence conditions (Cn^2 spanning two orders of magnitude), with photon-level validation over 750 m.
AI.result: Continuous secure-key generation was achieved with session-mean QBER of 5.6-6.8% across strong daytime turbulence to quiescent nighttime conditions; photon-level operation validated over 750 m free-space extension; all QBER values remained well below the 11% BB84 security threshold.
AI.conclusion: Secure photonic encoding conversion serves as a practical interface between fiber and free-space quantum communication platforms, preserving security assumptions by keeping converters as part of the untrusted quantum channel, providing a building block for future quantum networks.

title: Thermal Suppression of Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions in Finite-Dimensional Systems A Quasi-Hermitian Framework
summary: We investigate dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in finite-dimensional systems prepared in thermal equilibrium states and subjected to a sudden quench. A mixed-state Loschmidt amplitude is constructed from first principles within a metric-stationary pseudo-Hermitian framework, providing a self-contained derivation of the finite-temperature quench dynamics. Applying this framework to an $N$-level model consisting of a two-level sector coupled to $N-2$ spectator states, we find that temperature controls the DQPTs through the redistribution of thermal weights among the eigenstates. This mechanism leads to a dimensionality-dependent threshold temperature that becomes finite when the Hilbert-space dimension reaches five, above which the Loschmidt amplitude loses all real zeros and the DQPTs are fully suppressed. The thermal suppression mechanism suggests a general principle for controlling dynamical criticality through thermal occupation, while the quasi-Hermitian framework provides the self-consistent foundation for its rigorous derivation.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in finite-dimensional systems at finite temperature using a pseudo-Hermitian framework, finding that temperature can suppress DQPTs above a dimension-dependent threshold (occurring when Hilbert space dimension ≥5) through thermal weight redistribution.
AI.motivation: To understand how temperature affects dynamical quantum phase transitions in finite-dimensional systems prepared in thermal equilibrium, and to provide a self-consistent theoretical framework for analyzing finite-temperature quench dynamics.
AI.method: A mixed-state Loschmidt amplitude is constructed from first principles within a metric-stationary pseudo-Hermitian framework, applied to an N-level model with a two-level sector coupled to N-2 spectator states.
AI.result: Temperature controls DQPTs via thermal weight redistribution among eigenstates. A dimensionality-dependent threshold temperature emerges when Hilbert space dimension reaches five, above which the Loschmidt amplitude loses all real zeros and DQPTs are fully suppressed.
AI.conclusion: The thermal suppression mechanism provides a general principle for controlling dynamical criticality through thermal occupation, and the quasi-Hermitian framework offers a rigorous foundation for deriving this behavior.

title: Time-independent counterdiabatic driving for emergent two-level subspaces in many-body systems
summary: We show that geodesic motion in the Riemannian manifold of quantum states provides a direct route to time-independent counterdiabatic driving. Using the relation between the counterdiabatic Hamiltonian and the quantum metric tensor, we prove that a constant-speed geodesic makes the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of the counterdiabatic Hamiltonian constant. For effective two-level systems whose counterdiabatic correction has a fixed operator direction, this further implies that the full counterdiabatic Hamiltonian itself is time independent. We illustrate this result with the Landau-Zener model, three-level Stimulated Raman adiabatic passage and a collectively driven Rydberg ensemble in the blockade regime. Limitations of this approach in realistic many-body systems are discussed, where the two-level reduction is only emergent and leakage out of the effective subspace bounds the achievable speedup. In all cases, time-independent counterdiabatic driving achieves unit-fidelity state preparation on timescales substantially shorter than conventional adiabatic protocols while replacing temporally shaped auxiliary controls by fixed-amplitude fields.

AI.tldr: Geodesic motion in the quantum state manifold yields time-independent counterdiabatic driving by leveraging the quantum metric tensor. This approach achieves fast, unit-fidelity state preparation with fixed-amplitude fields in various systems, though limitations arise in many-body systems due to subspace leakage.
AI.motivation: To derive time-independent counterdiabatic driving directly from geodesic motion in the Riemannian manifold of quantum states, simplifying experimental implementation by replacing temporally shaped auxiliary controls with fixed-amplitude fields.
AI.method: The authors prove that constant-speed geodesic motion in the quantum state manifold makes the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of the counterdiabatic Hamiltonian constant, linking the counterdiabatic Hamiltonian to the quantum metric tensor. For effective two-level systems with fixed operator direction, this yields a fully time-independent counterdiabatic Hamiltonian.
AI.result: Time-independent counterdiabatic driving achieves unit-fidelity state preparation on timescales substantially shorter than conventional adiabatic protocols. Validated on Landau-Zener model, three-level STIRAP, and collectively driven Rydberg ensemble in blockade regime.
AI.conclusion: Geodesic motion provides a direct route to time-independent counterdiabatic driving, enabling fast state preparation with fixed-amplitude fields. However, in realistic many-body systems, leakage out of the effective subspace bounds the achievable speedup.

title: Unitary Synthesis with Near-Optimal T-Count for Near-Clifford Unitaries
summary: We present an approach to unitary synthesis that implements an arbitrary $n$-qubit unitary operator $U$ by a Clifford+T circuit with T-count $\widetilde{O}(2^n d_F^{\mathcal{C}}(U))$, where $d_F^{\mathcal{C}}(U)$ is the Frobenius norm distance of $U$ to the Clifford group. The T-count is shown to be near-optimal when $d_F^{\mathcal{C}}(U)$ is a constant. Our approach improves the previous best upper bound $\widetilde{O}(2^{4n/3})$ due to Tan (2025) for a large class of unitary operators $U$ as long as $d_F^{\mathcal{C}}(U) \ll 2^{n/3}$.

AI.tldr: A Clifford+T circuit synthesis method for arbitrary n-qubit unitaries achieving T-count ~O(2^n * d_F^C(U)), which is near-optimal for constant distance to Clifford and improves prior best bound ~O(2^{4n/3}) when d_F^C(U) << 2^{n/3}.
AI.motivation: To reduce the T-count (a costly resource in fault-tolerant quantum computing) for unitary synthesis beyond existing worst-case bounds, leveraging the unitary's distance to the Clifford group as a measure of "non-Cliffordness."
AI.method: Exploits the Frobenius norm distance d_F^C(U) from U to the Clifford group to bound the required T-count, using an approach that scales with this distance rather than worst-case dimension.
AI.result: Achieves T-count ~O(2^n * d_F^C(U)), improving on Tan's prior ~O(2^{4n/3}) bound for unitaries where d_F^C(U) << 2^{n/3}. The bound is near-optimal when d_F^C(U) is constant.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a tighter, instance-dependent upper bound for T-count in unitary synthesis, showing significant improvement for unitaries close to the Clifford group.

title: Heisenberg-limited metrology in the presence of non-Markovian noise with finite control rates
