summary: Recently, it has been shown that protocols utilizing infinitely fast controls, such as quantum error correction, can in principle restore Heisenberg-limited frequency estimation in the presence of a broad class of non-Markovian noise models arising from coupling to finite-dimensional environments. However, these controls differ substantially from those used to address Markovian noise, and their underlying physical mechanism remains unclear. In this work, we establish a direct connection between these protocols and the quantum Zeno effect, and extend the framework to infinite-dimensional environments. We delineate three types of constructions: (a) protocols that rely solely on measurements, (b) protocols using an active recovery after measurements and (c) protocols using dynamical decoupling and rigorously analyze the performance of each when controls can be applied at only a finite rate. While protocols relying purely on measurements can be engineered for noise models where active recoveries are fundamentally impossible, they result in the quantum Fisher information exhibiting a quadratically worse dependence on the control frequency. Surprisingly, while dynamical decoupling protocols are possible whenever protocols relying only on measurements can be engineered, the quantum Fisher information has the same dependence on control frequency as the active recovery protocols. Numerical simulations suggest that the improvement offered by dynamical decoupling may work in regimes beyond the perturbative setting where our rigorous theorems apply.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a direct connection between frequency estimation protocols using infinitely fast controls and the quantum Zeno effect, extending the framework to infinite-dimensional environments. It analyzes three protocol types (measurement-only, active recovery, dynamical decoupling) and their performance under finite-rate controls, finding that measurement-only protocols have quadratically worse frequency dependence, while dynamical decoupling matches active recovery performance.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical mechanism behind protocols that achieve Heisenberg-limited frequency estimation under non-Markovian noise, and to extend the framework from finite-dimensional to infinite-dimensional environments while analyzing practical constraints of finite-rate controls.
AI.method: The authors establish a connection to the quantum Zeno effect, delineate three protocol constructions (measurement-only, active recovery after measurements, dynamical decoupling), and rigorously analyze their performance under finite-rate control constraints using both perturbative analysis and numerical simulations.
AI.result: Measurement-only protocols show quadratically worse dependence on control frequency for quantum Fisher information. Dynamical decoupling protocols achieve the same control frequency dependence as active recovery protocols. Numerical simulations suggest dynamical decoupling improvements may extend beyond perturbative regimes where rigorous theorems apply.
AI.conclusion: The quantum Zeno effect provides a unifying framework for understanding these protocols. While measurement-only protocols are necessary when active recovery is impossible, dynamical decoupling offers a practical advantage matching active recovery performance without requiring explicit recovery operations.

title: Ancilla-Depth Phase Diagrams for Quantum Reference-Frame Comparison
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures; includes ancillary verification code and a deterministic regression certificate
summary: Comparing two noisy quantum reference frames as statistical experiments depends on the dimension of the ancillary memory available to the decision procedure. For finite-dimensional channels A and B with invertible A, we show that exact simulation of all measurements assisted by an r-dimensional ancilla is equivalent to r-positivity of the unique factor Gamma = BA^{-1}. The hierarchy can be realized by physical channel pairs: every unital, trace-preserving map that is k-positive but not (k+1)-positive embeds as the factor between the channels D_a and Gamma composed with D_a on an exact interval determined by the smallest Choi eigenvalue. For depolarizing source and target channels D_a and D_b, including negative and singular source parameters, the phase boundary is $\mathcal{D}_a \succeq_r \mathcal{D}_b \Longleftrightarrow -1/(dr-1) \leq b/a \leq 1$ for $a\neq 0$. We derive closed formulas for the restricted level-r deficiency and for the distance to every physical post-processing, $δ_{\mathrm{phys}}(\mathcal{D}_b\mid\mathcal{D}_a)=(1-1/d^2)\operatorname{dist}(b,I_a)$, where $I_a=\operatorname{conv}\{a,-a/(d^2-1)\}$. The largest physical conversion cost hidden from all tests through level k is $(d-k)/[d(d^2-1)]$. An untouched m-level spectator changes the first detecting external level from k+1 to $\lfloor k/m\rfloor+1$. A transpose--depolarizing construction shows that the separation is not confined to depolarizing factors. The results quantify the distinction between ancilla-restricted statistical simulation and implementation by a single quantum channel.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how the dimension of ancillary memory affects the ability to compare two noisy quantum reference frames as statistical experiments. It establishes an equivalence between exact simulation of measurements with r-dimensional ancilla and r-positivity of the factor Gamma = BA^{-1}, derives explicit phase boundaries for depolarizing channels, and computes closed-form expressions for deficiency and distances to physical post-processing.
AI.motivation: To understand the role of ancillary memory dimension in distinguishing and comparing noisy quantum reference frames, and to quantify the gap between ancilla-restricted statistical simulation and full implementation by a single quantum channel.
AI.method: The paper uses mathematical analysis with finite-dimensional quantum channels, focusing on r-positivity conditions, Choi eigenvalues, depolarizing channel families, and transpose-depolarizing constructions to characterize the hierarchy of simulation under ancilla dimension constraints.
AI.result: Exact simulation with r-dimensional ancilla is equivalent to r-positivity of Gamma = BA^{-1}. For depolarizing channels D_a and D_b, the phase boundary is D_a ≽_r D_b iff -1/(dr-1) ≤ b/a ≤ 1 (a≠0). Closed formulas for restricted deficiency and distance to physical post-processing are derived, and a transpose-depolarizing construction shows the separation generalizes beyond depolarizing factors.
AI.conclusion: The findings quantify how ancillary memory constraints create a hierarchy in quantum statistical comparison, with explicit critical values and phase transitions, demonstrating that ancilla dimension fundamentally limits the ability to simulate one quantum channel by another.

title: Logical Entangling with Phantom Codes in Hypergraph Products
summary: Logical entangling gates are a major source of physical spacetime overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computation. Phantom codes reduce this cost by implementing every ordered in-block logical CNOT through physical qubit permutations and Pauli-frame updates. Whether this mechanism can coexist with the low-weight stabilizer structure of qLDPC codes is a central question for low-overhead fault-tolerant architectures. We give a deterministic answer within binary CSS hypergraph product (HGP) codes. Up to natural equivalences, the simplex-repetition family is the unique HGP family satisfying the phantom condition. We then evaluate this family under circuit-level noise in logical GHZ-state preparation and Trotterized many-body quantum simulation. The codes retain low-weight stabilizer checks and yield concrete advantages over rotated surface-code baselines in both benchmarks. Reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays offer a natural setting for this approach, supporting nonlocal qLDPC operations while enabling in-block logical CNOTs without additional physical operations. Together, these results make precise how permutation-based logical entangling constrains code design within the HGP framework, demonstrate the circuit-level benefits of the unique family, and guide the search for phantom qLDPC families with better asymptotic parameters for low-overhead fault tolerance on neutral-atom hardware.

AI.tldr: Phantom codes enable logical CNOT gates via qubit permutations and Pauli-frame updates in fault-tolerant quantum computation. Within binary CSS hypergraph product (HGP) codes, the simplex-repetition family is uniquely identified as satisfying the phantom condition. This family retains low-weight stabilizers and outperforms rotated surface codes in GHZ-state preparation and Trotterized simulation under circuit-level noise. Reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays naturally implement this approach, offering a path to low-overhead fault tolerance.
AI.motivation: Logical entangling gates dominate spacetime overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computing. The central question is whether phantom codes' permutation-based mechanism can coexist with low-weight stabilizer structures of qLDPC codes to achieve low-overhead fault-tolerant architectures.
AI.method: The paper analytically characterizes all binary CSS hypergraph product code families satisfying the phantom condition, proving that the simplex-repetition family is the unique solution up to natural equivalences. Circuit-level noise benchmarks are performed for logical GHZ-state preparation and Trotterized many-body quantum simulation.
AI.result: The simplex-repetition HGP family is the unique phantom code family within binary CSS HGP codes. It retains low-weight stabilizer checks and yields concrete advantages over rotated surface-code baselines in both benchmark tasks under circuit-level noise.
AI.conclusion: Permutation-based logical entangling (phantom condition) tightly constrains HGP code design, identifying a unique viable family. The results demonstrate circuit-level benefits on neutral-atom hardware and guide the search for phantom qLDPC families with better asymptotic parameters.

title: Nonreciprocal Quantum Mpemba Effect
summary: We demonstrate a nonreciprocal quantum Mpemba effect. Consider a broad class of open quantum systems, each coupled to two isomorphic reservoirs through symmetric ports. Interchanging the parameters of the two reservoirs -- a discrete operation we call the swap -- turns the quantum Mpemba effect on or off without changing the initial states. The swap modifies the Liouvillian, yet a structural symmetry pins the eigenvalues while rotating only the eigenvectors. The nonreciprocity therefore leaves no trace in the spectrum and is carried entirely by the eigenvectors. Concretely, the swap alters the far state's projection onto the slowest mode, switching whether it bypasses the slowest relaxation channel. At a Liouvillian exceptional point, the far state's relaxation switches from bypassing the slowest mode to avoiding the critical slowing, with the on--off contrast intact. There the spectrum-independent mechanism takes its purest form.

AI.tldr: This paper discovers a nonreciprocal quantum Mpemba effect where swapping reservoir parameters turns the Mpemba effect on/off without changing initial states, driven purely by eigenvector rotation rather than spectral changes.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that the quantum Mpemba effect can exhibit nonreciprocity — being switchable on or off by simply swapping reservoir parameters — and to show this phenomenon originates from eigenvector structure rather than spectral modifications.
AI.method: The authors consider open quantum systems coupled to two isomorphic reservoirs via symmetric ports. They introduce a "swap" operation that interchanges reservoir parameters, modifying the Liouvillian's eigenvectors while preserving its eigenvalues due to structural symmetry. They analyze the far state's projection onto the slowest relaxation mode and examine behavior at Liouvillian exceptional points.
AI.result: The swap operation turns the quantum Mpemba effect on or off without altering initial states. The nonreciprocity is invisible in the spectrum (eigenvalues remain pinned) and is entirely encoded in eigenvector rotation. At a Liouvillian exceptional point, the far state's relaxation switches from bypassing the slowest mode to avoiding critical slowing, while maintaining the on-off contrast.
AI.conclusion: The nonreciprocal quantum Mpemba effect provides a spectrum-independent mechanism for controlling relaxation dynamics, taking its purest form at Liouvillian exceptional points.

title: Maximal Classicalization of Finite-Group Quantum Reference-Frame Noise
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. Ancillary verification code included
summary: A finite quantum reference token with group-valued misalignment induces a random-unitary channel, but optimal degradation is generally an optimization over all quantum post-processings. For a unitary representation U of a finite group G, we prove that the following conditions are equivalent: U contains every irreducible type; one ancilla-assisted input has an orthonormal G-orbit; signed group measures embed isometrically into channels in diamond norm; and, for every pair of noise laws p,q, $\inf_{Λ\in\mathrm{CPTP}} \frac{1}{2}\|Φ_q^U-Λ\circΦ_p^U\|_\diamond =\min_{r\in\mathcal{P}(G)}\frac{1}{2}\|q-r*p\|_1$. Thus representation completeness is the exact carrier condition for universal reduction of quantum post-processing to classical convolution. We determine the minimum ancilla dimensions for an orthogonal orbit and for an invariant calibration seed. For an incomplete carrier, with visible Plancherel dimension S(U), we derive the exact conditional-expectation distance $\frac{1}{2}\|\operatorname{id}-Φ_u^U\|_\diamond=1-1/S(U)$ and an explicit quantum--classical deficiency gap. For irreducible carriers the deficiency is obtained in closed form; the faithful two-dimensional representation of $S_3$ yields an exact ten-percent reduction relative to classical convolution. We also characterize law identifiability through the conjugation representation, provide finite linear programs and decision witnesses, and establish both a finite-dimensional obstruction and stable visible-band reconstruction for infinite compact groups. Deterministic ancillary code reproduces the finite-group examples and numerical regression checks.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that representation completeness (containing every irreducible type) is the exact condition for reducing quantum post-processing to classical convolution in finite quantum reference frames, derives closed-form distances for incomplete carriers, and characterizes law identifiability via group representations.
AI.motivation: To understand when quantum post-processing of a random-unitary channel (induced by a finite quantum reference token with group-valued misalignment) can be optimally reduced to classical convolution, and to characterize the fundamental limitations when the carrier representation is incomplete.
AI.method: The authors prove equivalence among four conditions related to representation completeness, use representation theory (Plancherel dimension, irreducible types, orthogonal G-orbits), formulate diamond-norm distances, and employ finite linear programs and deterministic ancillary codes for numerical verification.
AI.result: Representation completeness is equivalent to: containing every irreducible type, existence of an orthonormal G-orbit, isometric embedding of signed group measures into channels, and reduction of infimum over quantum post-processing to classical convolution. For incomplete carriers, the exact conditional-expectation distance is $1-1/S(U)$; the faithful 2D representation of $S_3$ gives a 10% reduction relative to classical.
AI.conclusion: Representation completeness is the necessary and sufficient condition for universal reduction of quantum post-processing to classical convolution; explicit gaps exist for incomplete carriers, and the framework extends to infinite compact groups with a finite-dimensional obstruction.

title: An Agentic Formalization for Certified Quantum Neural Network Design
summary: A central model in quantum machine learning is the quantum neural network (QNN), whose design requires balancing expressivity and trainability. Technically, expressivity is studied through circuit-function analysis, such as quantum signal processing, while trainability is analyzed using dynamical-Lie-algebra (DLA) methods. To support certified QNN design, we formalize these major components of QNN theory in a connected lean 4 development checked by a proof kernel, where every analytic input is either proved or exposed as a named hypothesis. On the expressivity side, we prove exact if-and-only-if characterizations of single-qubit QNNs, a resource-counted quantum phase processing theorem, and an overparameterization ceiling that bounds the quantum Fisher information rank by the DLA dimension. On the trainability side, we derive the direct-sum loss-variance law through a de-circularized second-moment interface. A parameterized Casimir-uniqueness engine discharges the required inputs for fully controllable, orthogonal, and matchgate circuit families, while single-qubit and product-Clifford ensembles close the two-design assumptions directly. A capstone theorem pairs the conditional variance law with exact loss reconstruction in DLA coordinates. The development record identifies eight corrections and clarifications that were not explicit in the informal arguments. We expect this work to provide a machine-checkable foundation for QNN theory and a step toward AI-assisted or automated design of quantum machine learning algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes quantum neural network theory in the Lean 4 proof assistant, providing machine-checkable proofs for expressivity (single-qubit QNN characterization, quantum phase processing, overparameterization ceiling) and trainability (direct-sum loss-variance law, Casimir-uniqueness engine, conditional variance law with loss reconstruction), uncovering eight corrections to prior informal arguments.
AI.motivation: Quantum neural network (QNN) design requires balancing expressivity and trainability, but existing theory is scattered across separate analytic frameworks (quantum signal processing for expressivity, dynamical Lie algebra for trainability). A unified, formalized foundation is needed to support certified QNN design and enable AI-assisted or automated quantum ML algorithm development.
AI.method: The authors formalize QNN theory in Lean 4, a proof assistant with a verified proof kernel. Expressivity is tackled via exact if-and-only-if characterizations of single-qubit QNNs, a resource-counted quantum phase processing theorem, and an overparameterization ceiling bounding quantum Fisher information rank by DLA dimension. Trainability is addressed via a direct-sum loss-variance law derived through a de-circularized second-moment interface. A parameterized Casimir-uniqueness engine discharges inputs for controllable, orthogonal, and matchgate families, while single-qubit and product-Clifford ensembles close two-design assumptions. A capstone theorem pairs conditional variance law with exact loss reconstruction in DLA coordinates.
AI.result: The formalization provides machine-checkable proofs for key QNN theoretical components. The development record identifies eight corrections and clarifications that were not explicit in prior informal arguments. The work establishes a verified foundation for QNN theory.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a machine-checkable foundation for QNN theory and represents a step toward AI-assisted or automated design of quantum machine learning algorithms, with the formalization uncovering subtle errors in prior informal reasoning.

title: The log log jam in Gaussian state tomography
summary:
Unlike in finite dimensions, quantum information in continuous-variable systems has the peculiar feature that without imposing physical constraints, the sample complexity of state tomography can be unbounded. Remarkably, this is even the case for state-of-the-art protocols for learning Gaussian states, which have finite-dimensional descriptions: the best known rates scale with $\log \log E$, where $E$ is the energy of the system. We prove this is not an artifact of existing analyses, but a fundamental limitation of the measurements used. We show: (1) Any protocol that uses Gaussian measurements, even entangled or adaptively chosen ones, must incur a $\log \log E$ dependence. This answers an open question posed by a number of previous works. (2) There is a smooth tradeoff between the number of rounds of adaptivity and the energy dependence, and we give a matching protocol achieving this interpolated rate. (3) With highly entangled, non-Gaussian measurements, one can learn $n$-mode pure Gaussian states with $O(n^2 / ε^2)$ samples, independent of $E$. This answers an open question posed by Chen et al. (4) A simple protocol based on the single-copy canonical phase POVM of Holevo and Helstrom learns single-mode pure Gaussian states with $O(1/ε^2)$ samples, again independent of $E$.
  Our results clarify the role of energy in bosonic state tomography and shed new light on the intriguing interplay between adaptivity, entanglement, and magic in quantum learning.

AI.tldr: This paper proves fundamental limits and possibilities in continuous-variable quantum state tomography, showing that Gaussian measurements incur a log log E sample complexity dependence on energy, while non-Gaussian measurements can completely eliminate this dependence. The authors establish a tradeoff between adaptivity rounds and energy dependence, and demonstrate that pure Gaussian states can be learned with energy-independent sample complexity using highly entangled non-Gaussian measurements or the canonical phase POVM.
AI.motivation: To resolve open questions about whether the log log E scaling in Gaussian state tomography is a fundamental limitation of Gaussian measurements or merely an artifact of existing analyses, and to determine if non-Gaussian measurements can overcome this energy dependence.
AI.method: The authors prove lower bounds for Gaussian measurement protocols (including entangled and adaptive ones), establish a smooth tradeoff between adaptivity rounds and energy dependence, construct a matching protocol for this tradeoff, and design two non-Gaussian protocols: one using highly entangled non-Gaussian measurements for n-mode pure Gaussian states (O(n²/ε²) samples), and another using the single-copy canonical phase POVM for single-mode pure Gaussian states (O(1/ε²) samples).
AI.result: (1) Any Gaussian measurement protocol must incur log log E energy dependence. (2) A smooth tradeoff exists between adaptivity rounds and energy dependence with a matching protocol. (3) Non-Gaussian entangled measurements learn n-mode pure Gaussian states with O(n²/ε²) samples, independent of E. (4) The canonical phase POVM learns single-mode pure Gaussian states with O(1/ε²) samples, independent of E.
AI.conclusion: Energy dependence in bosonic state tomography is a fundamental feature of Gaussian measurements, not a flaw in existing analyses. Non-Gaussian measurements (entangled or the canonical phase POVM) can eliminate this dependence entirely, revealing an intriguing interplay between adaptivity, entanglement, and magic in quantum learning.

title: A Noise-Aware Quantum Algorithm for Credit Valuation Adjustments on Real Quantum Hardware
comment: 56 pages, 14 figures, 18 tables. Includes supplementary appendices with implementation details, extended results, calibration data, and quantum-resource analysis
summary: Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) requires repeated risk-neutral expectation estimation, making it a natural test bed for quantum amplitude estimation, whose coherent amplification can in principle reduce Monte Carlo sampling cost. Whether this advantage survives realistic financial encoding and noisy hardware remains open. We develop an end-to-end, noise-aware quantum workflow for CVA, covering market calibration, discretisation, oracle construction, hardware execution and error-budget analysis. The model combines a correlated two-asset exposure with discount and default factors, encoded through a QCBM-based joint time-market distribution and controlled payoff rotations. We introduce contrast-aware Bayesian iterative quantum amplitude estimation (CABIQAE), which incorporates experimentally calibrated Grover-contrast loss into Bayesian inference and circuit-depth selection. Hardware-calibrated experiments show that CABIQAE exploits the limited amplification available on current devices more effectively than noise-agnostic alternatives and achieves a much lower classical post-processing runtime than the noise-aware BAE baseline. The analysis further decomposes the total CVA error into statistical, encoding, discretisation and hardware contributions. The full CVA oracle remains limited by circuit depth and discretisation resolution.

AI.tldr: This paper develops CABIQAE, a noise-aware quantum algorithm for Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) estimation that outperforms noise-agnostic methods on current hardware by incorporating experimentally calibrated Grover-contrast loss into Bayesian inference, while decomposing total CVA error into statistical, encoding, discretisation, and hardware contributions.
AI.motivation: CVA requires repeated risk-neutral expectation estimation, making it a natural test bed for quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) which can reduce Monte Carlo sampling cost. Whether QAE's advantage survives realistic financial encoding and noisy hardware remains an open question.
AI.method: Develops an end-to-end noise-aware quantum workflow: market calibration, discretisation, oracle construction (QCBM-based joint time-market distribution + controlled payoff rotations), hardware execution, and error-budget analysis. Introduces CABIQAE (contrast-aware Bayesian iterative QAE) that integrates experimentally calibrated Grover-contrast loss into Bayesian inference and circuit-depth selection.
AI.result: CABIQAE exploits limited amplification on current devices more effectively than noise-agnostic alternatives and achieves much lower classical post-processing runtime than the noise-aware BAE baseline. The full CVA oracle remains limited by circuit depth and discretisation resolution.
AI.conclusion: CABIQAE demonstrates practical quantum advantage potential for CVA on noisy hardware by effectively managing noise through contrast-aware Bayesian inference, though oracle depth and discretisation remain key bottlenecks.

title: Fixed-Boost Wigner Noise: Strict Trace-Distance Contraction without Quantum Degradability
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Ancillary verification code included
summary: A Lorentz boost acts on the canonical spin of a massive particle through a momentum-dependent Wigner rotation. We show that, for one fixed observer boost, reducing over an uncertain momentum can strictly contract every pairwise spin-state trace distance without producing a channel that is degradable from the less contracted one. For spin $1/2$, we first characterize the exact inversion-symmetric channel cone generated by a fixed Wigner angle and transverse momentum directions. Inside this cone lies the Pauli family $M_α=\operatorname{diag}(1-α,1-α,1-2α)$, $0\leqα<1/2$. For $0<α<β<1/2$, all trace distances between distinct spin states are strictly smaller after $M_β$ than after $M_α$, yet the unique linear post-processing factor has a negative normalized Choi eigenvalue. We solve the optimization over all physical converters exactly: $\frac{1}{2}\inf_{Λ\in\mathrm{CPTP}}\|Φ_β-Λ\circΦ_α\|_\diamond=\frac{α(β-α)}{2-3α}$, whereas the reverse deficiency is $β-α$. Thus the identity dominates the family, while all positive-noise members are pairwise incomparable under CPTP post-processing. The ideal construction is realized as the narrow-packet limit of pure, normalizable five-component momentum states, and explicit perturbation and finite-shot tomography bounds certify an open set of examples. Separately, every nonidentity member fails embedding in a time-homogeneous Pauli-diagonal Lindblad semigroup. Hence ordering all unassisted spin distinguishabilities does not determine the quantum statistical post-processing order.

AI.tldr: For massive particles, momentum-uncertainty-induced Wigner rotations can contract spin-state trace distances, creating a family of Pauli channels (M_α) where stronger contraction does not imply degradability or CPTP post-processing order; the identity channel dominates while all positive-noise members are pairwise incomparable, with explicit physical realization via narrow-packet momentum states.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether ordering all unassisted spin distinguishabilities determines the quantum statistical post-processing order, specifically by examining how Lorentz boosts with uncertain momentum affect spin-state distinguishability and whether stronger contraction of trace distances implies the existence of a physical (CPTP) map converting one channel to another.
AI.method: The authors analyze the effect of momentum-dependent Wigner rotations on spin-state trace distances under a fixed observer boost. For spin-1/2, they characterize the inversion-symmetric channel cone generated by a fixed Wigner angle and transverse momentum directions, identify the Pauli family M_α within it, compute the optimal CPTP post-processing factor (via diamond norm optimization), and realize the construction through narrow-packet limits of pure normalizable five-component momentum states with explicit perturbation and finite-shot tomography bounds.
AI.result: For 0<α<β<1/2, all trace distances are strictly smaller after M_β than M_α, yet the unique linear post-processing factor has a negative normalized Choi eigenvalue. The optimal infimum over all CPTP converters is (α(β-α))/(2-3α), while the reverse deficiency is β-α. Identity dominates the family, but all positive-noise members are pairwise incomparable under CPTP post-processing. Every nonidentity member fails embedding in a time-homogeneous Pauli-diagonal Lindblad semigroup.
AI.conclusion: Ordering all unassisted spin distinguishabilities does not determine the quantum statistical post-processing order, as stronger trace-distance contraction does not guarantee degradability or the existence of a CPTP map between channels.

title: Expressibility and trainability of a two-dimensional pairwise quantum-circuit ansatz
summary: Parameterized quantum circuits~(PQCs) constitute a central building block of variational quantum algorithms~(VQAs) and quantum machine learning~(QML) methods. Existing ansatz designs often adopt hardware-agnostic or simplified 1D chain/ring entanglement patterns. However, as quantum hardware continues to develop, native 2D connectivity patterns, such as planar superconducting-qubit architectures, are becoming increasingly important. Inspired by this hardware structure, we construct a native 2D pairwise ansatz and compare its expressibility and trainability with representative 1D ansatze at identical layer depths, despite their different circuit depths. For the fixed 16-qubit system, the 2D ansatz has the smallest KL divergence at $L=1$ and $2$, and its second-order frame potential approaches the theoretical lower bound more rapidly at shallow layer counts than the frame potentials of the three 1D ansatze. We also evaluate the gradient variance of the Pauli-$Z$-string expectation value $\langle Z_0\otimes\cdots\otimes Z_{15}\rangle$ with respect to the first $R_y$ angle. For this Pauli-$Z$ string and fixed parameter, the gradient variance is smaller for the 2D circuit at $L=1$--$4$. The differences narrow at $L=5$, and the four ansatze yield statistically compatible variances at $L=6$.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a native 2D pairwise ansatz for parameterized quantum circuits, inspired by planar superconducting-qubit architectures, and compares its expressibility and trainability against representative 1D ansatze on a 16-qubit system.
AI.motivation: Existing ansatz designs often use hardware-agnostic or simplified 1D chain/ring entanglement patterns, but with the development of quantum hardware featuring native 2D connectivity (e.g., planar superconducting qubits), there is a need to design ansatze that leverage such topologies for improved performance.
AI.method: The authors construct a native 2D pairwise ansatz and compare its expressibility (via KL divergence and second-order frame potential) and trainability (via gradient variance of Pauli-Z-string expectation) with three representative 1D ansatze at identical layer depths on a fixed 16-qubit system.
AI.result: At shallow layer counts (L=1,2), the 2D ansatz achieves the smallest KL divergence and approaches the theoretical lower bound of second-order frame potential faster than 1D ansatze. For the Pauli-Z-string expectation gradient variance, the 2D circuit yields smaller variance at L=1-4, with differences narrowing at L=5 and becoming statistically compatible at L=6.
AI.conclusion: The native 2D ansatz demonstrates advantages in expressibility and trainability at shallow depths, suggesting that leveraging hardware-native connectivity patterns can benefit variational quantum algorithms and quantum machine learning.

title: Spin Chain Quantum Communication on a Trapped-Ion Processor
summary: Efficient communication between distant qubits is one of the central challenges in scaling quantum processors. Although engineered spin chain protocols have been extensively investigated theoretically, their experimental realization has remained comparatively limited. Here, we experimentally realize engineered quantum communication protocols through digitally simulated spin Hamiltonian on IonQ's Forte 1/ Forte Enterprise 1 trapped-ion quantum processor. Combining exact numerical simulations with quantum hardware experiments, we benchmark uniform nearest-neighbour and engineered coupling profiles and demonstrate that engineered interactions significantly enhance the fidelity of quantum state transfer. We further show that exploiting the commutation structure of the spin Hamiltonian enables a parallel Trotter decomposition that more faithfully reproduces the target dynamics while substantially reducing the circuit depth and execution time compared to the conventional sequential implementations. Our results demonstrate that programmable quantum processors can effectively realize and efficiently implement quantum communication protocols, bringing Hamiltonian-based quantum communication closer to practical quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally realizes engineered quantum communication protocols on a trapped-ion quantum processor, demonstrating that engineered coupling profiles and parallel Trotter decomposition significantly improve state transfer fidelity and reduce circuit depth compared to uniform coupling and sequential implementations.
AI.motivation: Efficient communication between distant qubits is a central challenge in scaling quantum processors, and while engineered spin chain protocols have been extensively studied theoretically, their experimental realization has remained limited.
AI.method: The authors combine exact numerical simulations with quantum hardware experiments on IonQ's trapped-ion processor, benchmarking uniform nearest-neighbor and engineered coupling profiles. They exploit commutation structure of the spin Hamiltonian to enable a parallel Trotter decomposition that reduces circuit depth compared to conventional sequential implementations.
AI.result: Engineered interactions significantly enhance the fidelity of quantum state transfer. The parallel Trotter decomposition more faithfully reproduces target dynamics while substantially reducing circuit depth and execution time.
AI.conclusion: Programmable quantum processors can effectively realize and efficiently implement quantum communication protocols, bringing Hamiltonian-based quantum communication closer to practical quantum technologies.
